speechtext:

Then suddenly- what do you know?-while in Versailles, it finally sank through, and the minister told reporters that "we must do everything possible to improve the climate for investment." Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that there is virtually no action coming from the United States concerning the cleanup of chemical pollution in the Niagara River and the Great Lakes; in view of the fact that Lake Ontario will be dead in 20 years if these critical problems are not dealt with, and in view of the fact that Canada has been without an International Joint Commission chairman for months, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT ACTING PRIME MINISTER RECOGNIZE INEFFICIENCIES OF CORRECTIVE MEASURES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. It is now quite clear that the government is putting off making basic changes in its misdirected and injudicious economic policy because it would have us believe that the United States is the enemy and the cause of all our problems. Now that this subterfuge has been brought out into the open, is the Acting Prime Minister willing to admit that very precious time has been lost in putting off changes to the budget and the government's economic and energy policies, which for months have been shown to be totally inappropriate, and that this delay has caused a major increase in the unemployment rate?

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT ACTING PRIME MINISTER RECOGNIZE INEFFICIENCIES OF CORRECTIVE MEASURES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the answer to this question may be found in the press conference given by the Prime Minister yesterday in Paris. The Government of Canada has not accused the United States of having a high interest rate policy. In his press conference, the Prime Minister commented that the Americans themselves, the Secretary of the Treasury Mr. Regan in particular, have deplored the excessively high interest rates in the United States and said that these levels can be reduced only by Congress, and more specifically, by controlling the deficit. I therefore feel that my hon. friend is mistaken in saying that the Government of Canada is accusing the United States, while the same problem is being criticized in the United States. Have we lost precious time by not taking action? That is of course a matter of judgment, but once again, in his press conference yesterday, the Prime Minister said that we first had to know whether the Americans were going to act responsibly with respect to Canada's interests, and in that connection, he simply said that we could certainly not wait until November.

Madam Speaker, the rumours that are coming from the Summit conference indicate that the Minister of Finance is proposing to introduce significant changes in the anti-investment elements of his budget, that he is proposing to change the policy that has been followed toward foreign investment in this country, and also that he is going to attack the problem of the very, very high budget deficit which is currently approaching the $18 billion mark. These policies could have been attacked months and months ago. The only reason that we on this side of the House can see for the delays is that of using the many times discredited ploy of holding up the enemy outside as being the cause of
all our problems. Surely the minister understands this is not the reason for our problems today. Is the government going to persist in putting this slant on the problems when it presents its economic statement that is expected over the next few weeks?

Madam Speaker, once again, I must say that the assumption made by my hon. friend is false, since the Americans are as critical as we are with respect to high interest rates in the United States. In fact, statements by Mr. Regan, Mr. Haig and others clearly show that they, too, realize that the present interest rates in the United States are abnormally high. As for the intentions of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, I heard the rumours on the subject that were circulating yesterday. The Minister of Finance will be here tomorrow. However, I doubt very much whether he will be able to confirm or deny all these rumours, some of which are contradictory, but in any case, my hon. friend will have an opportunity to put his question to the minister directly.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is supplementary to those asked by the Leader of the Opposition. A few moments ago the Acting Prime Minister spoke of impressions. How much direct contact, if any, has he had with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance on what actually occurred in Versailles? Does he have any knowledge or authority to answer here in the House?
Finally, how much longer, given some time limit, will it take the government to come to the realization, and publicly admit, that the national energy plan and FIRA have driven out or discouraged billions of dollars in capital from our country in the name of Canadianization while discouraging foreign investments, and at the same time causing the Bank of Canada to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to prop up the falling dollar, which was caused by the government's economic illiteracy? How much longer will it take the government to realize and admit publicly that there has to be a policy change and will the minister give us some time-frame for a new budget and new taxation policies to spare Canadian taxpayers from this double-whammy?

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING CONTACT BETWEEN ACTING PRIME MINISTER AND CANADIAN DELEGATION AT VERSAILLES
speechtext:
On the first point, Madam Speaker, I repeat, knowing that the Minister of Finance will be here tomorrow, and knowing that he was involved in all aspects of the Versailles meeting, I thought it would be normal for me not to get in touch with him and take time from the discussions the Prime Minister and the Minister were having with other leaders. I thought that was the right approach.
With regard to the causes of the present situation, I think it came out very strongly from everything in the press that the "crisis" we are experiencing is not only a Canadian phenomenon. It came out very strongly that rates of inflation, rates of unemployment, were the same in every country-10 per cent, 9 per cent, 7 per cent, in countries which are used to much lower levels of inflation than is Canada. That particular dimension of it is pretty clear to me and to most people who read the papers during the weekend.

I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister if it also came out that Canada no longer has the luxury of pursuing narrow and ill-conceived Canadian nationalism at this time, that we no longer can afford it as a country? Did that come out?
Where? In the conversations at Versailles?
No, on the telephone.

On this subject, Madam Speaker, every person in Canada is slightly ambivalent. When the Minister of
Energy, Mines and Resources gives him or her figures about the higher degree of Canadian ownership in the petroleum industry, he or she is very, very pleased. A Canadian is equally pleased when he hears that some foreign-owned company is taken over by citizens of this country. Every Canadian quite normally hopes that more and more of that will take place, but quite rightly, in my view, he is not willing either to abandon some of the advantages that foreign ownership presents. All of us on this subject hope to have our cake and eat it, too; but most of us are pretty rational when it comes to having to make the decisions.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Transport. subsubtopic: REPORT OF NEGOTIATOR ON CROWSNEST PASS RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me indicate what would be the optimum scenario. I have a feeling-I am sorry I can only say that, because Professor Gilson is working, I was going to say frantically, but that is not true-he is working very hard to complete the report as soon as he can. The impression I have is that I will receive it in the next week or ten days. That is an impression only; it might be three or four, but it is coming. Second, it will then be translated and printed. It is expected that this will take two to three weeks, at the most. Then it will be made public, at that time, for people to comment on it.
Then cabinet will be asked to make decisions on it, before the summer recess. In August and September a draft bill will be produced, the bill will be presented to the House in the fall, and it is hoped that the program will come into operation in the new year.

Madam Speaker, since the minister was in Winnipeg not last week but the week previous to that, with Professor Gilson, it seems highly unlikely that he does not know generally what is in the report. Can he give an indication to the House of whether he expects to have general agreement on the recommendations that Professor Gilson will come out with, and whether or not he expects the government
June 7, 1982

will have to act unilaterally on some of the key issues of concern that Professor Gilson could not or may not have been able to solve in his negotiations?

Madam Speaker, I was indeed in Winnipeg and in Edmonton last week. I met with a number of people who have been in the discussions around Professor Gilson and all of them praised the tremendous knowledge and diplomacy that the professor brought to the meetings. Most of them said that the process of discussion was most educational for all those who took part. Will there be a consensus, will there be agreement by all sides to the recommendations of Professor Gilson-1 do not think so. There will be various degrees of support, and various degrees of lack of it.

The House resumed, from Thursday, June 3, 1982, consideration of Bill C-103, to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation, and Motions Nos. 4 and 5 (Mr. Hawkes).

Madam Speaker, the two amendments we are debating jointly are an attempt on our part to have the Liberal Party keep its promises. By voting for these two amendments, the only thing that will happen is that the promises made by the Liberal Party before, during and since the 1980 election will be kept. That is all that will happen. Those two amendments would have that simple little effect. The Liberals would keep their election promises.
The first amendment, Motion No. 4, would change the amount of the petroleum compensation charge from the current $75 per cubic metre to an amount not exceeding $28 per cubic metre. To put that in units most people understand, that would change the tax on gasoline, heating oil and diesel fuel from a 52 cents per gallon level to an 18 cents per gallon level. Your Honour will recall that in December of 1979, when the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) brought forward a budget proposing an 18-cent a gallon tax, the proceeds of which were to be used for subsidizing imported crude oil, the Liberal Party said that was too much. Hon. members opposite said that was outrageously high and that it was intolerable. Neither the Liberals nor their pink friends could live with that kind of tax level. That was outrageous.
You should turn red in the face when you say that.
That was outrageous, said the pinkies and the Grits. No, they could not tolerate that. There was no way they could tolerate an 18-cent a gallon tax. That was horrible.

You are a big blue movie that ought to be clipped.

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act

So the Liberals brought in a proposal of their own. They said we would have a made-in-Canada system. That used to be an honourable phrase. "Made-in-Canada" used to be something one could say with pride. It represented something of substance. What was the Liberal's made-in-Canada price system? Their made-in-Canada tax was 94 cents a gallon. They said that 18 cents per gallon was outrageous when that increase was brought in by the hon. member for St. John's West, but then the Liberal Party brought in an increase of 94 cents per gallon. When the bells started ringing and the public started to pay attention to what was in that atrocious energy package-that incredible abortion-and they found out that the Liberals were planning on 94 cents per gallon, then the government backed off and made it 52 cents per gallon. That is only three times as much as was considered outrageous in December, 1979, but that is how much the government backed off.
Motion No. 4 proposes that the government back off to 18 cents per gallon. The figure that was considered absolutely atrocious in 1979 is the figure they would be required to adopt today. If there are any Liberals over there who have any integrity-and that is not very likely-if there are any who feel an oblgiation to keep promises or a responsibility to honour commitments, if there are any such Liberals in the House like the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), then they have no choice but to support this motion. It asks nothing more than to reduce the maximum level of the tax to the figure that was found to be outrageous in December, 1979.
If hon. members opposite vote against this motion-and I am sure they will, being well-trained donkeys-then the public will have the proof that the Liberals lie, that they do not keep their promises, that they will say and do anything in order to achieve electoral victory. Afterwards they feel no responsibility and no sense of obligation.
The sad thing about this is that because we share the chamber with them, they bring contempt on all of us. Unfortunately, people tend to talk about politicians being dishonest. That is because of that kind of politics and those kinds of politicians, who make promises they know to be irresponsible and then shamelessly violate those promises.
This motion would give the government an opportunity to keep that promise. If there is any sense of decency among its members, they should vote for Motion No. 4. They would be doing nothing more than keeping the election promises they made so solemnly to the people of Canada in February, 1980.
Motion No. 5, which is being debated simultaneously, is also our attempt to keep the Liberal Party honest, futile as that effort may be. The motion attempts to limit the petroleum compensation charge to the amount that is necessary to fulfil the purpose for which it was intended. It was introduced as an item to provide revenue to subsidize imports so that we have one price across Canada. It does nothing more than say that is
the only purpose for which the petroleum compensation charge will be used and that it will not be used for generating funds for other purposes.
We have the solemn promise of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that that is all the charge was intended for-for this so-called "made-in-Canada" price, for oil subsidization. The problem with the solemn promise of the minister is that we have had solemn promises from Liberal energy ministers in the past few years that have turned out to be false, promises that were worth nothing. The promises the minister has broken, the statements he has made which have turned out to be untrue, follow the tradition of the Liberal Party in the last few years, and especially Liberal energy ministers who have performed in exactly the same way.
The minister's predecessor, the Hon. Alastair Gillespie, signed on behalf of the government an energy price agreement with the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia which called for the crude oil price to increase one dollar every six months. I think the provinces believed they had a contract with people they expected to behave honourably. However, in spite of those agreements, negotiated over many weeks and months with a lot of debate and which took a lot of energy, on September 27, 1978, Mr. Gillespie announced that the final one dollar increase would not take place. He was urged to break that contract by the New Democratic Party, which is as honest and respectful of contracts and agreements as the Liberals.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. In the House a member cannot allege that other members do things illegally, such as break contracts. In civil law that is illegal. The New Democratic Party has never advocated that contracts be broken. I spoke about that specific matter the other night. I wish the hon. member would get his facts straight and stop throwing mud.

Mr. Speaker, a Canadian Press report of 26 April, 1979, said that energy minister Gillespie had announced that the plan for a one dollar increase would not take place and that the New Democrats had urged cancellation of the previous increase. So, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Press reports that the NDP urged the minister to violate this written contract, and he apparently listened to their suggestions.

Before the hon. member alleges that we are saying the government should do something illegal, he should quote the reports correctly. They are changing a contract in consultation with the provinces, which I advocated and talked about the other night.

Mr. Speaker, we have from the record the fact that the immediate predecessor of the current minister of energy says that if the political pressures are such, he is quite willing to disregard a contract, break his word and tear up an agreement without being overly concerned about the consequences to the reputation of the federal government as an

institution which one hopes would obey the laws and respect the practices and traditions of this country.
Then, of course, we have the commitment of the Hon. John Turner, then minister of finance, who on page 31 of his 1975 budget said:
I therefore propose, effective tonight, a special excise tax on gasoline for personal use. The tax will be at a rate of 10 cents per gallon.
Earlier in his remarks he had said:
In recent months the gap between compensation payments and oil export charge revenues has grown rapidly. This has come about because the volume of our oil exports has fallen while our oil imports have risen.
So he had proposed this excise tax on gasoline in order to help subsidize imports. What has happened to that tax today, Mr. Speaker? I do not have the figures yet for 1981, but in 1980 that tax amounted to $441 million collected from Canadians. But what happened to it? It disappeared, Mr. Speaker, into the big pot. Is it used for import compensation as the then minister of finance said it would be? No, it is not used for that at all. It is gone. Canadian consumers are paying at least $440 million too much for their gasoline today because the statement made by the Hon. John Turner turned out over time to be false. Did he behave any differently from his colleague in the cabinet, the minister who succeeded him as the minister of finance, the Hon. Donald Macdonald? He is the fellow who, on September 13, 1973, unilaterally imposed a 40-cent export tax on every barrel of crude oil exported from Canada. He said that was to put in this two-price system. Then when the provinces objected he said on December 13: Well, we are going to give 50 per cent of that tax back to the oil-producing provinces and the rest will be invested in the industry, likely through a national oil company. Just two weeks later, on December 27-in between Christmas and New Year's which is guaranteed to be a time when most people will not notice-the export tax will rise to $6.50 a barrel and the commitment to return the tax revenues to the provinces will end when the tax technically ends and is replaced by a charge.
That is the kind of "honourable behaviour" you get from Liberals. They said: "Look, we made you a promise that we will share the export tax with you; the tax is ending on February 1 so there is nothing more to share. By the way, however, on the same day we are putting on a charge and we are going to keep it all ourselves." They changed the name from "tax" to "charge" and used that as justification for violating a commitment. Then they wonder why, Mr. Speaker, they have this legacy of mistrust, federal-provincial conflict, this ongoing battle between Ottawa and the provinces and the seeming inability of the federal and provincial governments to reach an agreement without having a battle first.
You cannot trust a Grit.

You cannot trust Liberal governments. They break their promises, break their commitments, and tear up agreements one after the other.
Is this minister any different? Let us look at a recent interview, April 2, 1982, on "Canada AM". The minister was asked by CTV interviewer Pamela Wallin:

CTV: The taxpayers in this country pay more than $6 million a day to subsidize oil imports yet, now to solve a problem, we have to increase our exports?

Now whatever we export is charged, there is a tax charge and the revenues coming from that export charge help in reducing our cost for the imported oil.
That statement, Mr. Speaker, is false. Not one penny from that export charge goes to help reduce the cost of imported oil. But it enabled the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to get out of a tight question in that interview, and that is what is important. The truth is not important at all. What is important is to get out of a box, and if you have to sacrifice truth in order to do that, so be it. Truth is not a commodity valued by the minister or this government.
This petroleum compensation charge, Mr. Speaker, was introduced by the government to give us a made-in-Canada price and supposedly result in Canadians paying less for their gas and oil. Our party recently did a survey of the price of gasoline in major Canadian and American cities. We compared the price in Toronto and Buffalo; Halifax and Boston; Vancouver and Seattle; Winnipeg and St. Paul, Minnesota, and Edmonton and Houston.
We are told by the Liberals that Canadians are protected from world prices because of the so-called made-in-Canada pricing system. That is what the minister tells us. That is what this government promised in the election campaign. Prices in the United States are deregulated. The Americans pay full price. They are not protected on the marketplace by their government. The world price dictates their price for gasoline and oil. With only one exception the price of gasoline in Canada is higher than in the United States.

First, by this amendment we seek to impose a limit consistent with all of the solemn promises made by the Liberal Party in the 1980 election. Second, through Motion No. 5 we seek to limit this tax only for that purpose. That is the intent of these two motions, which is then consistent with Liberal Party policy and commitments. If in fact the Liberals would like to live up to their commitments, they need do nothing more than vote for these motions and they will be honouring all of the commitments they made to the people of Canada.
There is one other item related to this petroleum compensation charge which should be brought to the attention of the House. It concerns the manner in which it was brought in at the outset and the manner in which it is accounted for in the accounts of Canada.
Let me deal with the manner in which it was brought in. The original petroleum compensation charge was introduced as a levy for the purposes of subsidizing Syncrude production. The House will recall that when the Syncrude agreement was reached, it was agreed to pay Syncrude world price for the synthetic crude that would be produced from that plant. That meant, therefore, that there had to be some subsidy for the synthetic crude to bring it to the lower level that was prevailing for Canadian crude. To achieve that the Petroleum Administration Act was introduced, which created a refinery gate levy, the proceeds of which subsidized the synthetic crude. That levy was brought in as legislation that had first, second and third reading. The money collected went into a special fund. This money was dedicated solely to subsidizing Syncrude production. However, the limit in terms of how much this levy might be turned out to be unsatisfactory. This should have necessitated an amendment to the legislation.
On July 11, 1980, however, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources tabled a piece of paper which he called a notice
June 7, 1982

of Ways and Means which raised this levy. This was an incredible procedure. The levy was brought in by legislation, but suddenly, in a piece of paper that was tabled in the House of Commons, the minister raised the levy. This was not a tax nor was it a budget statement. In fact, there was no statement. He just tabled a piece of paper indicating that the price would go up. It was incredulous, it was unbelievable.
We raised a point of order and the Chair said that it was a legal matter on which it could not judge. We sought a legal opinion and were told by legal counsel that what the minister had done was illegal, which confirmed our opinion. However, to pursue it through the courts would cost several tens of thousands of dollars, which unfortunately I do not have; in any case, it might end up with a Pyrrhic victory because the government might come along and retroactively make legal what was illegal. We have this incredibly arrogant attitude. The country is sick when the government blatantly, openly and with impunity breaks the law, which is exactly what the minister did, and apparently there is nothing we can do about it.
Just a few months ago I asked a legal officer of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in committee how the levy was changed or raised by just tabling a piece of paper, because it was not a tax and there was no tradition for doing so. He said that it was basically a tax. Then I asked why there was no Ways and Means motion preceding it in the first place, and he said that it was a procedural imperfection. Just like that, what had not been a tax became a tax! Is that not an absurd, asinine way to run the country? We are without any weapons to hold the government to account, to have it obey the law. Now it is a tax; suddenly it was changed from a levy into a tax. Because it is a tax the government has the ability to change its levels by tabling a piece of paper called a notice of Ways and Means.
Now it is a tax. Well, a tax is something which goes into the consolidated revenue fund and is accounted for through public accounts. Then expenditures by government through the blue book are funded by drawing on the consolidated revenue fund. Okay, we say that perhaps it has changed names and become a tax, but at least we have the knowledge that it goes into the consolidated revenue fund, that when it is spent it goes through the estimates procedure, that supply must be approved by the House, and that at least we will have an open and honest accounting of what is going on. Not at all, Mr. Speaker. When it comes to accounting, it goes back to becoming a levy.
How does the government do that? It is very simple. Referring to page 7-2 of the estimates for 1982-83, there is a line entitled "Payments to refiners and other persons who import crude oil and petroleum products", which shows $2,974,800,000 or almost $3 billion worth of expenditures. If we look down the list, we see another line entitled "Petroleum Compensation Revolving Fund", which shows a negative expenditure of $2,974,800,000. In other words, it is a revenue item in the expenditure accounts which cancels out the other
Petroleum Administration Act
expenditure. What effect does this tax and expenditure have on government spending? Nothing, zero; it does not show up.
When the Blue Book is presented, as it was at the end of February, the government has a lock-up for the media. Members of Parliament are not allowed in the same lock-up because we might talk with members of the media. Just the media is present, and high-priced officials prepare press documents for them. Then they announce to the world that government spending this year has risen 16 per cent over last year. This information goes out in all the stories over national television. This is what the people of Canada are told, and they believe it because their government tells them. In fact, if the government had not cooked the books with this little negative expenditure, spending had risen 22 per cent. We were deceived about this $3 billion expenditure.
It is a tax if they want to raise it, but when they have to account for it, it goes back to becoming a levy. If they do not want it to show up in government spending, they enter a little negative expenditure item so that a number is produced which looks nice and they can stand there and say, "We are restraining government expenditures; are we not good boys and girls?" If a private business tried that kind of creative bookkeeping, it would be in big trouble with the regulatory authorities. The Government of Canada does it all the time.
What, pray tell, can we do to keep the Government of Canada honest? Is there not a mechanism available to Members of Parliament to keep the Government of Canada honest, to keep it from cooking the books, and to keep it from changing taxes to levies and back to taxes at will, whenever it feels like it, so as to confuse?
Anyone who is concerned about what the government is doing with this petroleum compensation charge and the manner in which it has abused the House, the country, the electoral process and all of us who call ourselves politicians, by putting all of us into disrepute by its constant violation of promises, constant misinformation and distortion of the true facts of the situation, would join with us in voting for Motions Nos. 4 and 5 and in helping improve this legislation in just that little way. They do not cover everything that is wrong with the legislation-far from it. They certainly do not cover everything that is wrong with the National Energy Program-far, far from it. But at least it is a small step in the direction of being honest with the public of Canada and in fact doing what was promised in the first instance.
Before resuming my seat, let me indicate that this limiting of the petroleum compensation charge to a maximum of the equivalent of 18 cents per gallon will not result in any real loss of legitimate treasury funds because, if the government were to keep its promise that the export charge is to be used for import compensation, if the government were to keep its promise that the excise tax on gasoline would go toward import compensation, and if it directed the petroleum compensation charge toward import compensation, there is more than enough money to compensate imported crude oil so that we have a one-price system across Canada.

In no way can this motion be construed as somehow causing the government to be forced to dip into non-petroleum revenues in order to subsidize consumption in this country. All that this motion would do is cause the Liberal government to live up to its promises and nothing more. I do not believe this is an outrageous step to ask members of the Liberal Party to take, to live up to their promises-or at least this one promise.

It perhaps might be forgivable for the Canadian government and provincial governments to have loaded up with taxes if there was at least the decency to be honest about it. They should at least have had the decency to be honest and to say it was putting on these taxes for those reasons. But it certainly is an affront to decency and an affront to the House for the government, its spokesmen, minions and ministers to stand up and say they are protecting Canadians from world prices through the made-in-Canada price. Nothing could be further from the truth. It is not protecting anyone from anything. It is, in fact, bleeding the consumers for the benefit of the treasury in a dishonest way.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to this bill. I have heard this controversy between the Conservatives and the Liberals over oil prices for some time. Last weekend I attended a reunion of high school friends in Perth, Ontario. Most of the people there were from Mississauga, Oakville or west Toronto. It was very interesting to talk to those people. They are family people who are in their middle and late thirties and hard working. Frankly, they think we in the House of Commons are crazy when they see us yelling at each other and making great unsubstantiated charges. They are also worried about high prices and would like us to do something about them.
When I heard the last hon. member go on to rail about the opposition and when I heard the replies, it reminded me of a quote from Macbeth:
Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player That struts and frets his hour upon the stage And then is heard no more. It is a tale Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury,
Signifying nothing.
Instead of some sound and fury, today I would like to try to give some facts concerning the petroleum compensation charge and blended oil policy. I notice that the critic for the Conservatives has left so I hope some of his colleagues will take this message to him, because I want to compare Liberal and Conservative oil prices right now, and I would like the other parties to reply, if they can.
As of June, 1982, the Liberals' blended or consumer price per barrel is 75.8 per cent of world price. A blended price is taking Canadian oil, which is lower than world price, and world price oil, which we have to import because we do not have enough Canadian oil. We exported most of our cheap oil in the early seventies, adding on the various taxes, levies and charges, and then blending them all together and getting a price at the pump. The Liberals promised that the blended price would not exceed 85 per cent of the world price.
The Tory budget of 1979 promised that the Canadian price would not exceed 75 per cent of the world price from 1979 to 1982 and 85 per cent of that price from 1983 to 1984. The
Petroleum Administration Act
Conservatives also added an 18-cent a gallon excise tax on the gasoline. What we must remember is that it is a wrong impression when my friends to my right, the Conservatives, say: "Well, we were just putting 18 cents on". They put 18 cents on right away and then they were to make an agreement with Alberta and the other producing provinces and the price would have gone up and up. Likewise, the Liberals have made an agreement with Alberta and the other producing provinces which also makes the price go up and up.
I stand to be corrected, if I can be, but my comparison shows that as of June, 1982, this month, Liberal prices are approximately 41 cents a litre for regular gasoline, amounting to $1.85 a gallon. That varies slightly, up and down. Conservative prices would have been 42.8 cents a litre, or $1.92 a gallon. Therefore, it seems to me that the Conservative gasoline prices would be 7 cents a gallon more than the present price.
Talk about home heating oil.

The hon. member asks me about home heating oil. I think the Conservative price for home heating oil would have been less than the present Liberal price, because there was no 18-cent a gallon excise tax on that.
And gas?
It may have been slightly less than that for natural gas. But the point is-
The point is-

Wait a minute. Perhaps the hon. member would let me finish. The other point one must consider in the equation is that the Conservatives also promised an energy tax credit which would have given some money back to low and middle-income families, although we really never knew the nature of the credit. That must be considered. But the point is that both the Liberal and Conservative Parties are high-cost parties. They are approximately the same. So to spend 20 hours slinging darts or arrows at each other across the floor of this chamber is rather useless, it seems to me. The consumers are still getting hosed and there is nothing to help them.
The hon. member who spoke for the Conservatives tried to put blame on our party for breaking contracts. We never suggested breaking any contracts. In July there is to be another increase to $2.25 a gallon for gasoline. We said that that increase need not come, that there could be negotiations with the provinces to stop that increase and to give the consumer a break. That is what the consumer needs, a break. We gave the oil companies a break the other day. We gave Imperial Oil and its friend $2 billion and we gave them a break. We could find that money. This is what The Globe and Mail had to say about that in its article on June 3: "Imperial Oil Limited of Toronto is one of the big winners in the federal petroleum industry relief package." Sure, some small industries benefited and they needed to benefit from that, but the big boys also benefited. They were not happy. Shell's reaction was this, according to the Canadian Press: "Shell Canada

Petroleum Administration Act
Limited said Ottawa's $2 billion aid package for the industry is modest in scale and temporary in nature and will not significantly increase exploration in western Canada".
When I met with my friends this weekend at our reunion, as I mentioned, they asked me how the government could find $2 billion for the oil companies. They said, "The government is not taking any action against bank profits and we do not get anything. Our oil prices have gone up a great deal." As a matter of fact, they were right; their oil prices have gone up an average of 30 per cent in the last year. I have in my hand some statistics. The price of home heating oil went up from $770 a year to $1,100 for the average family. The price of gasoline, as I said, went up from $730 to $945 for the average motorist. That is substantial.
Who gets most of it?
My friend asks who gets most of it. Well, the industry gets a lot of it and I will tell hon. members why.
Most of it.

The government gets a lot of it, too. The industry gets most of it because it found oil when it was really cheap, $2 a barrel, and now it will sell that oil on the market for $30 a barrel. So they are getting a windfall there. There is no doubt about the fact that they are getting the money.
Who else is getting money? The federal government is getting money. The hon. member and I will agree that for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to stand up in this House and say that it is all the fault of the provinces is sheer nonsense. There is a federal excise tax. As the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) pointed out, the government extended that tax. The minister could cut back that tax if he wanted. The provinces, too, are villains. The Government of Ontario, the hon. member's province, tagged on an ad valorem tax. It got into the grab for money, too. The governments are grabbing the money, the oil companies are getting some money and the consumer is getting hosed. It seems to me that the facts are there.
I have in my hand a list of price increases under this Liberal government which I would like to read, but I get tired when 1 read it. There were two increases on August 1, 1980. There were increases on October 28, 1980, November 1, 1980 and two increases on January 1, 1981. There were increases on March 1, 1981, May 1, 1981, and two on June 3, 1981. There were increases on July 1, 1981 and September 21, 1981. The list goes on and on.
Keep reading.

The price of oil has risen from $14 a barrel to $30 a barrel. We know two things. We know that Canadians were living in a bit of a fool's paradise in the sense that we had oil prices which were too low. We know that western Canada is entitled to adequate compensation for its oil and gas resources. We knew the prices would rise. We should be honest with the people and tell them what they will rise to and let us not pretend, as the Liberal Party is pretending-
The Tories told them.
The Tories were not being honest. I just pointed that out.
Oh yes, we were.

Well, the hon. member has listened since the beginning of my speech and can reply to it. The impression I get from this debate on Bill C-103 is that the Conservatives are saying, "We would have put on only an 18-cent a gallon tax." That is not true. They would have put substantially more on. As a matter of fact, as I have said, their price would have been 42.8 cents a litre today.
The Liberals made a promise that we would have low oil prices and they broke that promise. They are not, perhaps, being straightforward enough to say so. I will give Your Honour an example of where they are not being straightforward. The headline of an article from The Citizen dated March 2 states, "Lalonde offers hope of cheaper gas". That is what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said. He said that Canadians may get a slight break at the pumps because international prices are going down and the government might consider reducing the special tax it levies to subsidize gas prices in eastern Canada. That is the petroleum compensation charge that we are debating today. Then last week, when he gave $2 billion to the oil industry, the minister said that the consumers will not benefit. I meant to say that he said the consumers will not hurt. They will not benefit, obviously, but they will not get hurt. He said there would be no change for the consumer. He did not say to forget about cheaper gas. The money being collected under the petroleum compensation charge will be in surplus. It could have gone to reduce the charge to the consumer. However, it will stay as a tax and the consumer will not get a break. Only one journalist, Les Whittington of the Ottawa Citizen, picked up what was happening to consumers. The rest of the press were misled by the slick press releases of Energy, Mines and Resources.
We have two parties essentially the same when it comes to oil prices, both protesting too much that they are low-priced parties. There is no relief in sight for the consumers. They will have a 30 per cent increase on their energy bill, and nothing to shield them from the worst.
There could have been a reduction in the petroleum compensation charge, but the minister will not do that now. The money will go to the industry. It will go to the industry because of the change in the price of oil, old oil discovered between 1973 and 1981.
Instead of the old oil price, it will be called an old-new price and they will almost get the new reference price. It sounds like mumbo-jumbo. It is an increase in price. It has to come from somewhere. It will come from the government forgoing lower prices to the consumer.
June 7, 1982

The government has to forgo other things as well. It will drop $25 billion in projected revenue because of the decrease in world prices and consequently the take for the government. That means the government will ultimately have to tax personal taxpayers more or forgo social programs. Either way the consumer gets hosed again. The consumer will get hosed at the gas pump, in his hydro bills, tax bills, and social programs. It is tough for the consumer.
I get back to my friends at the reunion. They need a little help. I will end on a positive note. The government could look at the petroleum compensation charge and at the agreement with the producing provinces. It could go back to Premier Lougheed and say that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Premier Lougheed made their champagne toasts over the oil price deal, clearly the small oil companies were stuck; and now that we have helped them, how about helping the consumers?
If the federal government cannot persuade Premier Lougheed, Premier Devine and Premier Bennett, then it should forgo its share of the new price increase coming in July. It would be a break, albeit a small one, for the Canadian consumer. The consumers are getting hosed and they need a break. That is what we should be debating here today instead of hurling insults at each other.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said that we were not honest with the Canadian people as to the prices they were going to have to pay for gasoline, heating fuel and natural gas.
Now, not then.

We were completely up front with the Canadian people. We were completely up front with the Canadian people in the Crosbie budget. We said exactly what we would charge in terms of a gasoline charge and exactly that the consumer would have to pay for home heating fuel and natural gas. We told the Canadian people the prices that would be paid for crude oil over the next four and a half years.
We were completely up front, completely honest and open with the Canadian people, as distinct from the point made by my colleague for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) with regard to the Liberal government. This government was completely dishonest. It misled the Canadian people. It is quite unfair for the member of the New Democratic Party to put us in the same boat with the Liberal Party.
I am talking about now, not then.

The Liberal government prices for heating oil are much higher than those introduced in the Crosbie budget. Natural gas prices are also much higher. We had an energy tax credit for all low and middle-income families in Canada. There is no such tax credit offered by the Liberal government.
If the hon. member wants to talk about fairness, let him be fair and put all the facts on the table, not just those facts he wants to impute to us which put us in the same boat as those rascals across the way.
Petroleum Administration Act
Further, the oil industry in this country would not now be lying devastated and in ruins had we followed the 1979 Crosbie budget instead of the Natural Energy Program we have today. Alsands would be two years further down the road. We would be well on our way toward an additional 260,000 barrels a day of oil and oil self-sufficiency in this country. If the hon. member wants to tell the truth, he should tell the whole truth and not just part of it.
The other night the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) went to great pains to tell Canadians what a great thing his National Energy Program was. He said that it was working beautifully for everyone, that it was glorious and that we were well on our way to energy selfsufficiency. The minister said that we have low prices and that Canadians have the best of both worlds. Why? Because of his National Energy Program, which he says has been glorious. He failed to mention, however, that it has caused a good deal of our unemployment problems. He conveniently forgot that it has contributed in no small way to high interest rates in this country.
More than anything else, the Liberal government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources do not understand that because of the National Energy Program, investors do not trust the government any more. They do not trust it because it has changed the rules in midstream. It has confiscated the assets of investors. Therefore, they do not believe the government.
For quite a few years before becoming a Member of Parliament, I was in business. Like most businessmen, I guess, I made a few mistakes here and there, perhaps more than some. I was in the oil well drilling business. I could drill 100 wells per customer and not make one single mistake. Every well would go according to program. One day I drilled a bad well. The 101st well was a bad one. We had problems, some within my control, some not. However, I was always remembered by that customer, not for the 100 good wells but for the one bad one.
That is the problem which this government and other governments face today. Investors do not trust it. Why would anyone want to invest in Canada when this government has confiscated the assets of people and changed the rules in midstream? It expropriated their assets. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) shakes his head and says they did not confiscate anybody's assets. What about when the government backed in to the Canada lands for 25 per cent? That is expropriation. That is what investors call it. Expropriation, without compensation; that is confiscation. Why would someone not invest in Canada? Investors do not have faith in us, that is why. They do not believe what this government is saying.
It has diminished cash flow. People invested their money in Canada to expolore for oil and gas. Then two levels of government come along once they find oil or gas and they take all

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
their money away from them. They do not leave anything that gives them a decent return on what they have already invested. It is a sad thing today.
The reason the National Energy Program, for some Canadians, seems to have sold so well is just that the oil companies seem to be bad guys. They are the scapegoat, so then the National Energy Program must be good. That is the tragedy. Most Canadians automatically think that Imperial Oil, Shell, Gulf are ripping the people off; therefore Petro-Canada must be good. What a sad, sad story.
The people of Canada put up $600 billion of their hard money for the privilege of buying their gasoline at Petro-Canada stations. Do they get it any cheaper? Is one cent a gallon any cheaper? No, they pay the same. But that is only the half of it: there is no return on that $6 billion, either. It is just going down the tube. Petro-Canada came out with a great big statement saying how much money they have made. Any other company in Canada that made as little money on $6 billion as Petro-Canada makes would not be in business, let alone have anyone investing in it. Petro-Canada is a criminal abuse of taxpayers' money, and Canadians will have to wake up and understand that that is what is contributing to the high interest rates.
Where do hon. members think the Government of Canada is getting that $6 billion? Do they think they just manufacture it out of thin air? They had to go out and borrow it, because the Government of Canada could not tax the people enough to pay for it. When you go out and borrow $6 billion, you have to pay the going rate of interest.
Interest rates, whether we like it or not, are a function of supply and demand. If you buy a car or a house today, or if you buy food for your table, what you pay is a function of supply and demand, and interest rates are just that. So the $6 billion that is being poured into Petro-Canada is causing the Canadian people to pay 17 per cent, 18 per cent, 22 per cent rates of interest today on their homes and cars and credit cards.
We are not going to get this country back on the rails until governments, and particularly the federal government, recognize one fundamental issue, that until you have investor confidence people will not invest. When you do not invest, not only are we not creating jobs for ourselves, but we are not creating jobs for our kids. We are losing jobs because people are taking capital out of the country. Ten billion dollars went out of Canada last year, $10 billion that could have created
200,000	jobs.
Until the federal government and other governments recognize the investor and treat the investor fairly, we will not create jobs, we will have further unemployment, we will have higher interest rates.
As for the National Energy Program, or the update thereof last week, I said that the minister seemed to blow his horn, trying to tell the Canadian people what a glorious success this had been and what the National Energy Program had done for
all Canadians. But if you do not have the cash, you offer some incentives, some modification to the program. For example, for the small Canadian oil or gas company the government offered a credit against the PGRT of $250,000 a year. That is quite a bit of money: it represents one 5,000-foot dry hole.
They don't even know what that is.

That is what $250,000 will buy you, Mr. Speaker. We have 400 oil and gas companies in western Canada, so we can drill 400 more dry holes a year. We cannot complete them, but we can drill them.
People are not going to drill. Taking a man's cash flow away from him is like walking into your neighbour's house and stealing his silverware, and then coming back and saying: "I am sorry, here is your silverware back that I took last week".
The point is that the oil and gas industry does not have the available cash flow to go out and drill for new oil today. The new oil prices are attractive, I grant you that, and some of the incentives are attractive; but you must have the cash in the first place to go out and drill for that new oil. If you do not have the cash flow, you are not going to do it.
Apart from the petroleum and gas revenue tax relief of $250,000 a year for each individual oil and gas company for a period of four and one-half years, apart from that one tax concession, all of the other concessions were made for a period of one year. When you go out to look for an oil and gas well that you hope will produce for 15 years, or perhaps 20 years in the case of gas, you do not predicate your investment decisions on one year. When you are going to invest the kind of money that it takes to find an oil well or a gas well, you predicate that investment on a tax regime that will be in place for at least the term of payout, which is at least seven, eight or ten years. How can investors have any confidence in a program or a tax modification which amounts to saying: "We will change it for a year, then we will have a look at it, and if we do not like it we will change the rules back again". How can you reasonably expect any investor to have confidence in such a program? It is ridiculous.
The devastation the government has caused in the industry in my province, Alberta, by virtue of the National Energy Program is really sad. Here was an industry that was providing jobs not just for the people in Alberta, but it was the only industry that could have helped Canada through this period of recession. I do not say it would have solved all of the problems, by any means, but it certainly would have helped. Many people who do not have jobs today would have jobs. It would not have solved our high interest rate problem, but our interest rates would not have been quite so high without the National Energy Program.
For every $100 that is spent in the oil and gas industry in Alberta, only $29 stays in the province; $71 goes to other provinces. And $41 of the $71 goes to the province of Ontario alone. For every one job that is created in the oil and gas industry in Alberta, two jobs are created in the province of Ontario.
June 7, 1982

What this government has done has caused sadness not just for Albertans but for all Canadians. I keep asking myself whether it was by design or by accident. Was it the deliberate intention to destroy the oil and gas industry in this country, or was it just because hon. members opposite did not know any better? I see my hon. friend smiling. Has he asked himself that question? If it was done by design, I think that is pretty frightening.
All the jobs lost in Quebec, and he laughs.
My hon. friend laughs at that proposition.
Be serious.

Since I came here three years ago it has been my understanding that the fondest hope of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal government and one of the Prime Minister's cherished dreams was to unite this country. I tell my friend that he has done more in the last three years to take this country apart than has been done in the last 15 years.
Rubbish.
The sad part of it is I do not think my friend even knows what he has done; nor does he have any appreciation of it.

speechtext: What have you done in this country other than spread that type of nonsense?
What have I done?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Want an election?
Right now!
Nineteen eighty-four.

If we were the government today, we could put this country back together on a solid footing, which is something that hon. member does not have the courage to do. Hon. members opposite do not have the necessary gumption; nor do they understand the problem.
You gave away the store.

This afternoon we are debating Bill C-103, which is part of the National Energy Program. It is a bill which will completely overhaul the Petroleum Administration Act and change its name to the Energy Administration Act. The maximum allowable oil export charge will be raised to $55 a barrel. The charge will be determined by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources instead of by the National Energy Board. We set up the National Energy Board to look after these determinations for us, but the government does not like that. The government does not like the independence of the National Energy Board. We gave the National Energy Board too much authority, so we are going to take that away so that the minister can set these charges by order in council. The government will be permitted to return 50 per cent of the proceeds to the producing provinces if it sees fit.
Petroleum Administration Act
A transportation fuel compensation recovery charge can be applied to all aircraft and ships leaving Canada. In practice, the charge will no longer be applied to foreign aircraft companies. A petroleum compensation charge can be levied to a maximum of about $12 a barrel in order to pay oil import compensation. By the insanity of our National Energy Program we are importing 400,000 barrels of oil a day into Canada, and we have 300,000 barrels of oil shut in in western Canada trying to find a market. We are paying $40 a barrel every day for 400,000 barrels while we have 300,000 barrels in the ground out in western Canada. What kind of absolute irresponsibility is that? It is just incredible. The government says we have commitments to foreign suppliers. Perhaps we have, but how long would we be paying for foreign oil imports if the compensation charge was reduced? At the same time, surely to goodness, could we not reasonably expect that the government would not mind allowing western Canada to sell
300,000	barrels of oil to the United States? The United States is importing 5.5 million barrels of oil every day, 300,000 barrels of it from western Canada. But no, the government thinks we should keep it shut in. "Let's keep our thumb on those westerners; let's not give them a break."
Bill C-103 gives retroactive authority to the government to introduce a special compensation charge for any cutbacks in western Canadian oil, and the bill allows the government to levy a Canadian ownership charge to a maximum of $1.15 a barrel and to a maximum of 15 cents per MCF of natural gas. The tax ceiling would have been $4 a barrel under the previous legislation, and the proposed Energy Administration Act would establish the Canadian ownership account into which the funds would go. Further, the proposed Energy Administration Act would give the government the authority to amend the pricing terms of the Syncrude agreement.
The motions we have before us this afternoon are Motions Nos. 4 and 5, and my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary Centre, has explained the purpose of those motions. The purpose of Motion No. 4 is to reduce the maximum level of the petroleum compensation charge, in effect to 18 cents a gallon, which would correspond with the 18 cents a gallon set forth in the Crosbie budget. By passing this amendment, hon. members opposite at least would be saying to the Canadian people that they have not exceeded their election promise of 1980. I think my colleagues have explained that.
Motion No. 5 would limit the petroleum compensation charge so that it could be used only for purposes of subsidizing imported crude into Canada. It would not be allowed to be moved over to the Consolidated Revenue Fund or to be used for other purposes.
Those are the two motions we have before us this afternoon and, in my view, they appear to be quite reasonable. I see no reason why anyone should object to them.
I just want to say a further word about the National Energy Program while I have the floor. One of the stipulated intents of the National Energy Program was to provide energy security

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
for Canadians. I have spoken about some of the other tragedies of the National Energy Program in terms of its devastation, the unemployment it has created and so forth, but in my view the greatest tragedy to the Canadian people of all is in terms of energy security or security of supply of oil. We in Canada rely very heavily upon oil. We rely on it to the extent that over 50 per cent of all our energy consumption in Canada is oil-related. As I have said, we import 400,000 barrels of oil of the approximately 1.6 or 1.7 million barrels of oil consumed per day. We are importing 25 per cent of our oil.
Through the National Energy Program the minister told Canadians we would have security of energy supply. That is a fraud, because the National Energy Program is depriving Canadians of oil security. Our reserves are diminishing at a very fast rate. We produce about 1,200,000 barrels of oil per day out of a total of 1.6 million that we use. We import the balance of 400,000 barrels a day. Our conventional oil reserves are declining at the rate of 100,000 barrels per day per year, so in ten years our conventional oil and gas fields will be capable of producing one million barrels per day less than they are producing today. If we do not find any more oil, our conventional oil fields will only be capable of producing about
200.000	barrels of oil per day by 1990.
The government should tell that to Canadians. Instead, it tells people not to worry because it will be possible for them to substitute gas for oil. The government feels confident that people will conserve a lot more oil. Last year for the first time people practised conservation and consumption was reduced by 7 per cent. But the easiest part of conservation is over, Mr. Speaker, and the easiest part of substitution is over.
I say the government is practising a fraud on the Canadian people by insinuating that they will have oil security. I wonder how much of last year's 7 per cent saving was attributable to the recession? I wonder if we really conserved anything or if that 7 per cent was all due to the recession.
Assuming that oil consumption does not increase one barrel between now and 1990 and that we are still consuming
1.600.000	barrels per day then, our conventional fields will only be able to produce 200,000 barrels per day. So we must ask where the other 1,400,000 barrels will come from. Will they come from Hibernia, from the Beaufort Sea, from the megaprojects, the oil sands? The minister did not say anything about that the other night, not a word. He implied that we will be secure because the government will continue to make substitution possible. Does he mean that will come by conversion to gas, Mr. Speaker? In his wildest dreams does he believe that he is going to be able to substitute natural gas, coal and electricity for 1,400,000 barrels of oil per day? He does not have a shred of evidence to support that claim that he is willing to put before the Canadian people or this House. I wonder who we will buy that oil from in 1990? At the moment we buy from Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Mexico. Even if they are able to sell it to us then, I wonder what price we will pay? Will it be $40 per barrel or $100 per barrel?
When we have the opportunity in Canada to be self-sufficient, why would the government introduce a National Energy Program that would deprive us of that opportunity? I cannot understand that and my constituents cannot understand it. Why would the government be so hidebound, so doctrinaire, as to introduce a program that will deprive Canadians of the opportunity to achieve self-sufficiency? No one will explain that to us.
Bill C-103 and all of the National Energy Program was never intended to come to grips with the primary goal of selfsufficiency. That is just a nice set of words used to describe the government's main intent, which was complete control over the oil and gas industry and to siphon off huge amounts of revenue so that it could continue with its profligate spending. In the forecast of revenues over the next five years the government includes $53 billion from the industry. It might not be so bad to destroy an industry if that $53 billion were used to create jobs and help bring interest rates down. But that is not the case, Mr. Speaker.
The second priority of the National Energy Program, which the government ranked ahead of self-sufficiency, was Canadi-anization of the industry. With the introduction of Bill C-103 and other parts of the National Energy Program, Canadians are witnessing a new era in which government not only shares the planning function with business, but where government actually makes the business decisions for the industry.
This bill, together with others, is the most massive, coordinated program of regulation, tax measures and other interventions aimed at moving the government to the position where it virtually controls every single aspect of the industry. We are about to see, or probably have already seen, a bureaucracy of accountants and lawyers the like of which we have never seen before to administer this legislation. By virtue of these regulations the government will control the day to day decisions of managers in the oil and gas industry. The substance of this legislation, in many cases, is such that companies and individuals are guilty unless they can prove themselves innocent. Public servants are placed in the position of making recommendations which will depend on highly discretionary choices between different proposals.
In short, Mr. Speaker, what we have is government bureaucrats who will be directly involved in commercial decisionmaking. I say we are dangerously close to becoming a socialist republic. In one form or another the new regulatory moves are designed to gain complete influence and control over business decisions. As I said, these regulatory measures have been coordinated with a host of other programs, like the changes to the tax regime which are designed radically to increase the fiscal take of the government.
It is hard to imagine the administrative burden which all these regulations will place on the industry. The cost of doing business will be increased to a staggering level-indeed, it already has been. The cost of compliance with the new information requirements for COR, PIP and PMA will be out of all proportion to the economic benefits derived. Time, manpower and money will be spent filling out forms instead of being

devoted to production activities. Rather than an oil and gas finding operation the industry will be turned into a bookkeeping operation of lawyers and accountants.
Let us look at what happened in 1981 as a result of the NEP. We know the industry is lying in ruins. We know exploration in western Canada has fallen by 30 per cent. We know the Cold Lake and Alsands projects are dead. We know drilling in western Canada fell from 9,000 wells in 1980 to 6,600 wells in 1981. We know that last year our imports of crude and refined products averaged 418,000 barrels a day. We know the federal government paid out $4.5 billion last year to refiners to offset the extra cost of imported crude. We know that industry cash flow declined by 35 per cent during the year, with earnings down a similar amount. We know that $10.2 billion left the country. We know that because of the government's Canadianization policy more than $7 billion of that $10.2 billion went to acquire assets of foreign-controlled companies. We know these purchases created a burden of debt which seriously hinders future oil and gas exploration and development, and they did not add one single barrel of oil to our energy reserves. We know that $3 billion left Canada to explore for oil and gas in the United States and elsewhere. These companies are exploring for oil and gas in other countries and we are still importing 400,000 barrels of oil a day. It is madness. This large outflow of capital is one of the major factors in pushing the value of the Canadian dollar to a 50-year low and interest rates to a record high.
What about the oil well and drilling rigs service industry? Here was a Canadian industry, 90 per cent owned by Canadians. What has happened to them? Twenty-three companies are bankrupt today by virtue of that government. Two hundred and twenty-seven rigs have left the country, mostly for the United States. One hundred and seven oil well servicing rigs have left the country. Of the 461 rigs left in Canada, there were 121 working last week. In June, 1980, prior to the NEP, there were 360-odd rigs working in Canada. Industry has lost
25,000	jobs. Thousands of professionals engaged in the industry have left our country, driven out by a senseless and inane government.
Is it any wonder that we see this hostility and bitterness in western Canada toward the federal government? The Prime Minister in a speech not so long ago blamed racism for the election of a separatist to the Alberta legislature. Just how far out of touch can the Prime Minister be to make such an assertion? He cannot have any appreciation whatsoever of the alienation felt by western Canadians caused by his dogmatic approach to the Constitution, the NEP and the Crow rate. The election of a separatist in Alberta has absolutely nothing to do with racism. It is a sad indictment of our Prime Minister that he should so gravely mistake the enormity of the feeling which exists in western Canada today. If he or any of his cabinet would spend even a little time listening to the people in western Canada and remove themselves from their centralized isolation in Ottawa, they might learn that there is serious-very serious-trouble brewing on the prairies. I do not say this in any sense as a threat; I say it because this government has turned
Petroleum Administration Act
its back on the people of western Canada and they feel helpless with nowhere to turn. Believe me, I have never seen the level of frustration and desperation which exists in Calgary today.
The minister of energy had a press conference last Friday. In his opening statement I read this:
We today introduced legislation to implement the final major elements of the National Energy Program designed to give Canadians control of their energy future and ensure self-sufficiency in oil by 1990.
The people of this country do not believe that. They do not believe this government. The minister may believe it, but he is the only one. I sincerely hope the Beaufort and Hibernia will eventually produce enough oil for us to be self-sufficient. I think the potential is there, but it will not happen by 1990, and for the minister to pretend it will is a serious misrepresentation of the facts to the Canadian people and he knows better. In looking at the amendments to Bill C-103, I would hope the government will have enough courage and wisdom to accept the amendments and throw out the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I got involved in this debate earlier through a number of interjections and a couple of questions, and I want to round that off by making some brief observations. I want to restrict my remarks to the issue of price, which was raised a short while ago by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and then commented on by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).
I do not debate the conclusion that prices generally appear to be higher in Canada at the pump than they are in the U.S. I have heard enough evidence from learned members of this House and interested constituents to convince me of the accuracy of that observation. The point of my original interjection was to ask why the price was higher, because it was argued that the reason was the policies of this government. If you look at the price of gasoline when it leaves the refinery in both countries, Mr. Speaker, 1 think you will see a substantial difference. I think any objective and honest member of this House would agree that at that point Canadian prices, at about 75 per cent of the world price, are far cheaper than their American counterparts.
If that is the case, why do Canadians have to pay more at the pump than the Americans do? The answer is obvious, and in a way it was contained in the response that I got from the hon. member for Calgary Centre. It lies with the high provincial taxes that we have in many provinces in Canada. If we are looking for a culprit to blame for higher prices, and that seems to be the intent in many debates in this House, I suggest you do not have to look any further than, say, Bill Davis in Ontario and John Buchanan in Nova Scotia. Mr. Davis, as everyone knows, recently introduced a 20 per cent ad valorem tax on gasoline. That accounts for the higher price of Ontario gasoline compared to its counterpart in New York state. Premier Buchanan in Nova Scotia just introduced the 15-cent a gallon tax in Nova Scotia, which accounts for the higher Halifax price compared to the Boston price. _

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
Having commented on the arguments developed by the Conservative spokesman this afternoon, I would like now to pass on to the arguments presented and developed by the spokesman for the New Democratic Party. First, I will comment briefly on the preface to his remarks, when he reproached us gently about the unseemly squabbling which characterized the interaction between myself and the hon. member for Calgary Centre. I could not help but smile inwardly as I compared the rhetoric with the apoplectic intervention by the hon. member several days ago when he rose continuously in this House on points of order, attempting to score points against the very member who was the object of my interjections this afternoon. Perhaps the hon. member had a brief or a selective lapse of memory when he brought the Shakespearean reproof to our attention this afternoon.
The New Democratic Party is attempting to pose as the low-price party in this House during this debate. I would like to point out that I have to doubt the honesty of that posturing and I do so based on two arguments. The first argument arises out of the fact that the New Democratic Party is, in essence, a western party. It may have an eastern leadership, but it is in fact a western caucus. I do not believe that any party that is so dominated as that party is by its western members could convincingly argue to anyone, at any time, that it could negotiate a cheaper price with the western premiers and with its western constituents than we did or the Conservatives thought they did.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
I do not buy that argument at all. I do not think anyone else who has looked through the debates of this House over the preceding two years would buy that argument either.
Second, the New Democratic Party is a very ambitious party. The members of that party have had the courage of their convictions to outline in this House, in some detail the energy policies they would execute if only, through some miracle or divine intervention, they formed the Government of Canada. If you review the list of policies which they are proposing, Mr. Speaker, you would find that they are very expensive proposals. I would ask the hon. member or the audience beyond this House how on earth the New Democratic Party expects to pay for those ambitious expensive policies. I suppose that it would not impose the cost at the pump. In not doing that, the party could lose as a low-energy-price party. But someone, somehow, somewhere, at some time, will have to pay the price of its energy policies. I would argue that if you are not paying for those policies at the pump, as we are asking the consumer to do for many of our policies, you will be paying for those policies through your taxes.
You got it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
For hon. members of the New Democratic Party to argue that their party is a low-energy-price party when, in
fact, it would be socking it to the taxpayer for the most expensive energy policy of all the three parties constitutes, I think, a ludicrous and farcical assault on the very honesty which that gentleman attempted to bring to this debate a few moments ago.
