speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay)-The Economy-Query respecting contact between Acting Prime Minister and Canadian delegation at Versailles, (b) Pursuit of Canadianization policy; the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid)-Astra Trust-Position of depositors, (b) Minister's statement; the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell)-Status of Women-Parliamentary report on battered wives-Government action.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-103, to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation, and Motions Nos. 4 and 5 (Mr. Hawkes).

Mr. Speaker, in rising to deal with the propriety and wisdom of Motion No. 4 and Motion No. 5 placed before this House, I might comment initially upon the remarks made by the energy spokesman for the New Democratic Party, to whom I listened with considerable interest. It seems convenient for members of that party to recall part of the facts but not all. It was not until the hon. member was reminded of the specific plans we had when we formed the government to include an energy tax credit, which would have been of substantial benefit to a great number of Canadians, that reference was made to that specific proposal when he compared prices of the Liberal Party today to prices proposed when our party formed the government. We had to be reminded also that the 18-cent federal excise tax of 1979 was not to apply to home heating fuel.
The issue before the House is not to compare energy policies of 1979 with energy policies of today because the public, the
June 7, 1982

final juror in determining the merits of the 1979 tax proposals, made its decision. That decision is one we cannot question. The issue surely before the House today is whether the proposals contained within the ambit of Bill C-103 are effective in implementing a program promised the Canadian people when their votes were cast in February, 1980, and whether that program is in line with specific commitments which have been made and whether they are in order today. The answers to those questions are most definitely not so.
I can recall vividly my experience on the election platforms prior to the February, 1980, election when I was advised by my Liberal opponent that the consumer in Canada would be confronted with a blended petroleum price and that was easily explained, said he, as being a combination of three specific prices; the price for conventional crude oil, the price for synthetic crude and the price for imported foreign oil.
I raised the question at that time that one of the constituent elements of the price happened to be an unknown quantity, that of the price of imported foreign crude over which this government has no control. Under those circumstances, how could he then assure my constituents that the price which would be paid by them would be less than the price they were then paying? The promise was, "Vote Liberal and the price will stay down".
The one component of that composite price which was never mentioned, although it should have been obvious to all, was the petroleum compensation charge, an equalization charge which permitted Canadians from coast to coast to pay relatively the same price for a gallon of gasoline, a gallon of crude oil or a gallon of diesel fuel. We are looking at that obvious omission today, the public already having been subjected to some impositions of the same nature as those which related to the Alberta levy to compensate for a cutback by the province of Alberta in two of three stages. The crucial issue was the commitment of the current government, in the words of a specific advertisement during the time of the 1980 election in the riding of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), to "vote Liberal and the price will stay down." What was omitted from the campaign literature was the small print, which should have read: "until the Liberal government takes office." The print was so small that it was not seen, and the public believed.
The proposals which we have before the House with respect to Motion No. 4 would have the effect of reducing the petroleum compensation charge from the current $75 per cubic metre to $28 per cubic metre. That change would result in a reduction in the price per gallon from 52 cents to 18 cents, an amount which will correspond to the amount of excise tax to be used for the purpose of paying the petroleum compensation charge referred to in December, 1979, and an amount above which the new Government of Canada pledged itself not to go. Accordingly, it is appropriate to point out that the entire amount, as it currently stands, is a reduction from the originally sought amount by the government of 95 cents per gallon.
Petroleum Administration Act
After the nights and days of the long bell, that amount has been reduced.
This piece of legislation is but one of a series of bills which have resulted from that action, an action which, incidentally, even in terms of the bill as it presently stands, has had the effect of saving the consumer of Canada, who may have driven on an average of 12,000 miles per year and derived 25 miles per gallon from his vehicle, $201 in the course of a year on his gasoline consumption. In the event that this specific proposal in Motion No. 4 should be passed, the additional saving to the same consumer, driving the same number of miles per year and deriving the same miles per gallon, would be $163 per year. That is not an insignificant amount. It is one which could be better used in the hands of hard pressed-consumers of Canada than in the Consolidated Revenue Fund maintained by the government.
I listened with some considerable interest to the comments of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) when he stood in his place last week and announced some adjustments to the National Energy Program. It was of significance that in the course of his address he made no reference to two most significant circumstances which had developed since the announcement of the NEP. Those circumstances were the abandonment of both the Alsands and Cold Lake projects, after the Government of Canada had pumped $50 million into the accounts of Imperial Oil for the purpose of shoring up a plan which ultimately was to fail. The money was badly spent because, throughout its negotiations with the province of Alberta and with the province of Saskatchewan, the government had adopted a stance of confrontation, the same kind of confrontation politics it adopted in dealing with the province of Newfoundland with respect to the Hibernia issue and generally with respect to the province of Quebec. The entire western part of the country has been abandoned to confrontation and bitterness, a fact which quite frankly is well known to some government members who have raised this very issue with their government but with no results. It is fundamentally important to the country that the benefit of all Canadians be looked to. That can never happen if the national government picks a fight with every province at every turn to get its own greedy way. Its own greedy way has been to take more and more of whatever is left in the pockets of consumers.
In 1917 the Government of Canada of the day imposed a tax which took effect in 1918. That act became the Income Tax Act of today. It was a temporary, war income tax measure designed to raise revenues for a specific purpose for a limited period of time. The Government of Canada soon recognized that it had found eldorado. This system of regularly and consistently extracting funds from the public, first of all in small amounts and then gradually in greater and greater amounts, was the salvation to the rapacious appetite of the federal government. The government today has given new meaning to the words "black gold".
The oil which is generated and produced in western Canada has become a new eldorado for the federal government. It has tapped into that resource to the extent that originally it

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
anticipated, generating over a five-year term $53 billion. The government was to get it in a variety of ways-compensation charges, Canadian ownership charges, royalties or levies. Whatever it might call them, they were all a form of taxation. When a government reaches into the pocket of a citizen and extracts therefrom an amount, that amount, properly given its name, is a tax. To call it an ownership charge, to call it a petroleum compensation charge, or to call it a donation to a benevolent fund, is frivolous and deceitful. It is purely and simply a tax. That tax has grown and will continue to grow under an administration which recognizes that it has a new source of wealth which it can tax and indirectly take from the pockets of the taxpayers and consumers of Canada without their intimate knowledge.
The government's convenient metric system which it uses to determine the charges that are made is part of the program to confuse the taxpayers so they do not know how much they are paying. In order to determine an amount which taxpayers will understand, it is necessary for someone to sit down and calculate exactly what $75 per cubic metre is. When all of that is done and government members stand in their place to claim that the provinces have imposed a special road tax or ad valorem tax, such as that Ontario has placed on petroleum products at the pump, they fail to mention that of all the entities deriving part of the final sale price of a gallon or litre of gasoline, the one with the biggest hands and longest grasp is the federal government. As of March this year, fully 34.5 per cent went into the hands of the Receiver General for Canada.
The issue of the ad valorem tax imposed by the province of Ontario is one that I lament. I do this because it adds a tax to another tax, which adds to inflation. It is a signal to the public that governments believe that tomorrow's price will be higher than today's price. If that were not so, why would anyone impose an ad valorem tax? Governments expect the price to be higher tomorrow. However, in doing so the provincial government has but followed the lead of the federal government, which did the same thing with its excise taxes.
When those issues were debated in the House, I drew to the attention of the Minister of Finance what the consequences would be. There is an alleged battle between the government and inflation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told us as recently as last weekend that it is true that you can wrestle inflation to the ground so long as you wrestle the economy to the ground. He has accomplished the latter but has failed in accomplishing the former. Nevertheless, it is measures such as this which fuel inflation. The government is taking more and more instead of less.
How can the hard-pressed consumer expect to pay for the increased costs that are imposed upon him by a government when he has less money as a consequence of specific programs which are advocated and undertaken by the government to extract more from the pocket of the consumer, who is left with less to pay with? That is the result. It is deceitful then to turn around and say that its battle is with inflation, and to say to
Canadians; "You have too great a demand upon the public; working as you are, you should reduce your demand on the economy because in that way we will achieve our desired goals of combatting inflation". The greatest contributor is the federal government itself.
This measure but adds to inflation. It takes more from the public and adds it to the consolidated revenue fund, but not as a charge or something which can be specifically identified for a certain purpose and allocated and invested in the interim to generate income to be used for the purpose of paying the alleged levy. The charge is quite clearly a simple form of taxation. We have a perfect example of how the measure is ineffective in terms of meeting a specific commitment.
It is to this issue that Motion No. 5 is directed. When we examine how Clause 40 of the bill has been drawn up, we see that it was designed to offset the cost of additional petroleum compensation payments that had to be made to Canadian refineries when it became necessary to import more foreign crude to offset the loss of Alberta crude. That Alberta crude diminution, the House will recall, resulted from a failure of the government to negotiate an arrangement with the producing provinces of the west which would have obviated the need for ever imposing that charge.
In any event, what are the facts as they surround this particular circumstance? We are asked to pass a measure to allow for a certain amount to compensate for that special petroleum compensation payment made to the refineries. Since we know the period that it covers, the amount of oil that had to be imported as well as the specific amounts which had to be paid to the refineries, we can determine that this specific provision of the bill as it stands today generated $142 million more than was required. The specific provisions are designed, as I have indicated, to cover the shortfall in Alberta production. Yet $142 million more was raised to cover the 120,000 barrels a day than was needed.
The interesting fact in all of this is that at the very time that these charges are to be imposed, that is, effective March 3, 1981, until September 21, 1981, the actual consumption of petroleum products in Canada declined by more than the
120,000	barrels a day for which this compensation is allegedly imposed. I would have thought that the Government of Canada, if not recognizing that that reduction in consumption should immediately offset the Alberta charge, should have at least prorated the amount. But it did not because it has one conception of all charges, levies and amounts. The conception is that these are all forms of taxation which provide an opportunity to grab from the public. Why diminish the appetite of the government at all? It can surely spend that somewhere else.
This brings us to a very significant point in this entire issue which was discussed in some detail by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) when he directed the attention of the House to the fact that when these charges are shown in the public accounts they are not reflected as revenue imposed upon
June 7, 1982

the taxpayers on one side and as an expenditure of the government on the other, but as a flow-through in which the Government of Canada is treated as a conduit. It is taking from the taxpayers and paying to another. But if that be true, then there should be no $142 million surplus, because the whole justification for the approach taken is that what we have taken from one group of taxpayers we have paid to another. But that is not the case.
It is deceitful, to be kind to the government, to proceed in this fashion. It underlines the fallacy of the entire concept. Whatever government takes must be shown as revenue derived, and whatever government spends must be shown as an expenditure of government. There is no flow-through. There is no conduit pipe. If this concept is given the full extent to which it may be taken, can Your Honour not conceive of the Government of Canada raising a special tax which it might call the "Canadian Benevolent Fund" which would be used to pay the salaries of public servants? Since it would be a special imposition under the conduit pipe concept, the accounts of this country need never show the payment of a dime to the public service of Canada.
The whole theory is deceitful. The government must disclose what it really spends. In terms of these revenues, it has spent over $3 billion in compensation. What it has retained in the Consolidated Revenue Fund is another form of tax which was not distributed to an alleged recipient at all. These measures become essential at a time which is most crucial to all Canadians, when our economy is suffering and revenue could best be left in the hands of Canadian business and Canadian taxpayers generally.
The Prime Minister has acknowledged that we have an economic crisis. He made that acknowledgment in Versailles over the weekend. One wonders whether he learned that only when he arrived in Versailles or whether he knew it before he went. If he knew it before he went, why has he not done something about it other than to sit in this House with his colleague the Minister of Finance explaining that we are waiting for the Americans? We have been waiting for the Americans for over a year. He wants to wait for the Americans for another six weeks. Wait for them to do what? This is a sovereign government. We need not wait for the Americans to do anything. The people of Canada elected this government for the purpose of taking specific measures with respect to the economy and their hopes for the future. It was not elected as a surrogate of a government in another country. Yet if we listen to the government ministers, they would have us believe that they are powerless to do anything, that they can do nothing but wait until they are in a position to transmit to the Canadian public whatever decisions may be made in a foreign country. If that be the case, why do we need the Minister of Finance? Why do we need the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources extracting funds of this kind? Why can we not simply rely upon the administrators in a foreign country. The Canadian people are not prepared for that. They expect action.
I submit that of all the action which can be taken, the most crucial is certainty. We have been waiting since November 12,
Petroleum Administration Act
1981, for a bill to amend the Income Tax Act. One would have thought that that piece of legislation would have been before the House long before now, but it has not come. In the result, Canadian businessmen have declined to take any action, hoping that the measures which were anti-business, antiinvestment and anti-enterprise will be changed. And there was change. They are wise to wait, but waiting is costly for the entire economy. Precision and certainty are absolutely required. This delay, the delay of the year, and now the delay of six weeks, is inexcusable. Measures of this nature strike at the root of all our nation's problems. The government knows and has known for some long time that its economic policies are misplaced. They are for another time, another country, maybe another planet, but not for here and now in Canada. The government has not taken the decisive steps to build confidence. Instead, we are dealing with a piece of legislation which once again imposes additional taxes on Canadians.
These measures that our party recommends in terms of Motions Nos. 4 and 5 would, in the first instance, bring within the level of the promises of the government the price structure for petroleum products which resulted in part, and maybe in whole, in the government's election in 1980. The provisions contained within our Motion No. 5 would see to it that the revenues derived from the compensation levy were, in fact, no greater than those genuinely needed for the purpose of meeting the compensation payment to the refineries. How can any hon. member of this House who believes the purpose to be as set forth in the legislation object to and complain about that kind of logical restriction on the Government of Canada?

Madam Speaker, 1982 is the one hundredth anniversary of many towns in southeastern Saskatchewan and it is being celebrated by most of them this summer. One of the thoughts which will be in the minds of many people attending these celebrations is the background to these very motions we are discussing today. I speak with some personal knowledge of this, not only because my people came to Saskatchewan in 1882 when it was a territory of the federal government and went through that long period of struggle for self-government which came in 1905, but also because when I go back to check the statutes of that time, it brings back the names of men who sat in this House, of men who sat in the territorial legislature in Regina and of men who later sat in the legislatures of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The tragedy of that decision in 1905 to set up these two parts of the Northwest Territories as two provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, was cruelty of the highest order. It gave to these two new territories the right of self-government, but it did not give them the wherewithal to run those governments. The setting up of the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905 did not give to the pioneers of those territories, to keep them out of the hands of the Americans, the right to own their own resources. These people had to fight with railways and grain companies to survive, but it did not give them the rights to their own resources.

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
Every other province from 1867 had the right under the British North America Act to own and enjoy the income that came from its resources. Little Manitoba, little British Columbia, little Ontario and Little Quebec-and they were small provinces in 1867-had that right. Under the British North America Act, the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia were enlarged. They always had the resources, but Saskatchewan and Alberta did not.
This was remedied after a long battle. They won the battle of self-government, with no financial power, in 1905. It was remedied in 1930 by amendments to the British North America Act which gave to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan the right to own the properties in their provinces, the mineral, water and land properties, and to enjoy all the revenues and royalties from them. Any person who took those revenues was stealing. This is what happened in the period between 1905 and 1930.
The federal government retained those resources, as it does in the case of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Any revenues that came from that wealth went to the federal government and not to the people who lived in those territories. That injustice in 1905 has come back to this House today to haunt us.
I do not think the House would mind if the record showed what turned out to be, and I will quote from it, the Saskatchewan Act. This is the Saskatchewan Natural Resources Act which was an amendment to the British North America Act of 1930.1 will read just a few phrases:
And whereas the Government of Canada desires that the province should be placed in a position of equality with the other provinces of Confederation with respect to the administration and control of its natural resource as from its entry into Confederation in 1905-
After all those years as a territory and then as a partial province, it finally agreed in 1930 that this injustice would be remedied. It makes it very clear. I will just read a sentence or two. I quote:
the interest of the Crown in all Crown lands, mines, minerals (precious and base) and royalties derived therefrom within the province, and all sums due or payable for such lands, mines, minerals or royalties, shall from and after the coming into force of this agreement and subject as therein otherwise provided, belong to the province-
It was part of the Magna Carta of western Canada, in the parts called Saskatchewan and Alberta, that in 1930 in this House Parliament accepted this proposal and made the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta equal in rights and privileges to those of other provinces.
Today we are debating amendments to the Petroleum Administration Act in the form of two tax laws dealing with that act. I want to put very clearly to the House what the background and perspective is. I am not participating in the debate on the details of how these taxes are too high and for common interests, both economic and moral, we should reduce them. I want to talk about the fundamental, moral and legal principles that made this country.
In my opinion, the Petroleum Administration Act, which these two motions are in effect amending, is unconstitutional. I
said that at the time of the passing of the act in this House in 1974. I must confess that I got no support from lawyers on either side of the House or from the provinces when I pointed out that the Petroleum Administration Act was an infringement on the British North America Act.
The minute this Parliament said that under the Petroleum Administration Act of 1974 it was going to use the trading power of the federal government to overwhelm the property rights power of the British North America Act granted to the provinces, that, in my view, was unconstitutional. I do not blame the lawyers of this House or the lawyers of the provinces for being reluctant to get into this debate. Constitutional law is strange to the great majority of lawyers I know, certainly those in politics.
At that time I was sensitive to the fact that the Queen's property was being exchanged and moved around without the consent of the Queen, as the debates of 1974 will show, and that the House with its eyes wide open was warned about it. I must confess with sadness that the only people who seemed interested in my arguments at that time were the Clerks at the Table. I want to add a little more meat to that argument for the purpose of showing that some day this House will have to remedy the mistake we made in 1974 by going into the powers of the provinces laid down in the Constitution and for not having paid proper compensation for so doing.
I quoted from the statutes. I could quote similar phrases from the Alberta statutes and later amendments. However, the two constitutional arguments that were used were, first, that in the national interest the trading power of the federal government was superior to the property rights of the provinces. If you think about it, you realize the deep concern, I might say the alarming concern among various members of this Parliament from Alberta and Saskatchewan. They are very conscious of the fact that the property rights of the provinces were infringed by the Petroleum Administration Act and, of course, this tax under these motions. They know in their hearts that we have no right to steal the resources of a province without compensation.
The legal support for this is very simple. There are many cases in our courts which say you cannot do indirectly what you cannot do directly. Coming at it on the basis that the Petroleum Administration Act was in the public interest because there was an adjustment of prices going on in the world, that gave the federal government the power to move in and arbitrarily take control of the property of these provinces. Once you allow one level of government to get into the heartland of the other level of government, it is very difficult to take it out.
I listened to the hon. member from Calgary speak earlier. He posed the question: Was this action taken by Parliament deliberately or was it taken blindly, unknowingly? I, like him, do not know the answer. If I were to be truthful, I think many people have already decided what the answer is, namely, that with a little bit of time, there is a given group of people, mostly
June 7, 1982

in Ottawa, who seek and long for the day when the federal government will control not only the property all across the country but also the actions of the people all across the country.
There is much evidence to support this trend, both here and in the United States. In the current effort, we have our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) saying to the cattle producers that he will not help them because agriculture is a joint responsibility of both provinces and federal government, and until the beef producers bow their knee and accept the concept of a marketing board that will apply all across Canada and will control the production, sale and distribution of those animals.
Here we have a force loose upon the people, a force which emanated originally from Europe but which was known in North America 30 years ago. It has been accepted by a large group of civil servants in the department of agriculture in the United States, and it has been accepted by the civil servants in the Department of Agriculture in Canada, that the only way we can run the industry is to get control of the farmers' production and thereby direct things on a planned basis so that we do not have a surplus. We will get prices up by creating a scarcity; they call it supply management. They have it in the dairy industry today; why not apply it to the beef industry, they say? Most farmers, I believe, would not mind a marketing board if it were to market the stuff, sell it, under rules fair to all the participants. But the farmers do not want a board that is a controlled board, particularly one that is controlled by civil service experts-whose track record in Canada is pretty bad. Their track record in other countries is worse. We have seen the dairy industry lose 5,000 farmers a year; the civil servants simply put the dairy farmers on supply management. The beef farmer would rather go broke with his own mistakes than go broke with the mistakes of a group of people who are very good at drafting memorandums and regulations, and so on, but who have not got a sense of the situation and who believe they can take the Lord's place in this moving around in the market field.
I have no quarrel with the sincerity of these people. I am simply saying that there is reason to believe, in the minds of many of our people in Canada, that there are strong forces at work here in Ottawa, as well as in other places in Canada, trying to get control not only of the resource but of the people who produce that resource. I have not yet got to the stage where I can believe that those people are going to succeed.
In my own province, Saskatchewan, where this force is very strong, I saw a complete reversal of the majority vote in that province. I hope that the same feeling will eventually prevail in provinces like Ontario, on the same kind of decision we are discussing now. Put your mind to the question asked by the member from Calgary: Was this Petroleum Administration Act deliberately designed or was it an accident by people who do not know what they are doing? For the moment I think we had better agree, in the interest of respect for each other, that it was an accident by people who did not know what they were
Petroleum Administration Act
doing. The only way we can operate this House is by believing that that was the reason.
That does not change the fact that what we are doing by this amendment today is continuing the error of the original petroleum administration bill, which, 1 suggest, has some day to be fought out in the Supreme Court. That will have to be done by a reference from Parliament that asks the questions in clear and precise English that we can all understand, questions that ask the court to give us an answer in clear and precise English that we can understand, namely: Where do we stand on this question of property rights that are now within the realm of the provinces? Where do we stand on this priority of the trade power versus the property power? These are rather exotic subjects for this House. They can only be settled by the right type of reference, over an extended period of time, with the time to think it through.
We have a responsibility here as Members of Parliament. If the judges cannot make up their minds what we meant when we agreed to the British North America Act in 1867 and when we agreed to the Alberta and Saskatchewan acts in 1930, then we had better pass a resolution, with support from all sides, that tells the judges at all levels: "This is what we meant when we spoke in 1867 and this is what we meant when we spoke in 1930". This federation system, this federal system, cannot work unless there is a clear-cut understanding of what it means. When you give them powers to restrict the subject to one level of government, that must be honoured and not used indirectly to do something that cannot be done directly.
This is one of the reasons this whole discussion of the bill of rights which we had here for the last year or so was to me a complete fraud. Nothing has been done to clarify the rights of the provinces concerning their property. There is no use in trying to pretend to people that we are putting it into the bill of rights here federally, beause it will not make any difference until we make it clear in the minds of the judges where we stand, so that we do not get these silly decisions that we get from them occasionally.
Once again, the first point is the trade power versus provincial property rights. The second constitutional issue is the question of prices. We have always assumed that, by judicial decision only the provinces have the right to fool around and countrol prices and wages. We have always assumed that and taught our children in school that this was the law. The only exception to that law was where there was a national crisis, where we were in complete extremity, and all the rules go by the board. The only type of extreme necessity really comes down to a shooting war.
The House will remember the imposition of the War Measures Act in 1970. The plea that was made for breaking the laws of Canada was that there was an apprehended insurrection, and the army was moved in. They arrested several hundred people, that is all they could find, who might possibly be considered to be about to organize an insurrection; it turned out that there were only ten or 12 people that they could hold. So we had the shameful experience of seeing Members of

Parliament on both sides of this House supporting the government's imposition of the War Measures Act in a time of peace over a problem of a few social drop-outs.
That mistake should be written deeply into the minds and hearts of all of us because we were all guilty, with just a few exceptions, of making that mistake. We should remember- now that we are not in a period of apprehended insurrection or an immediate shooting war-that now is the time to get our thinking clear and to make sure the judges know what our thinking is on these fundamentally important things like property rights and the relative power of the federal government in times of crisis.
The Supreme Court was given a reference on this question of prices and ruled that there was a national emergency because oil prices had gone up. That is part of the background to the legislation we are now amending.
Any person knows-and every person should have known eight years ago-that there was no national energy emergency. This country and the United States had energy running out of our ears, and as long as the industry is nursed, we always will have energy running out of our ears. What there was was a price adjustment. We had been stealing oil from producers, mostly the Arabs but also the people of Alberta, Venezuela and Nigeria, for over 50 years, and the rule of law on prices was set around the world by seven big international oil companies. All this is in the record. The producers to whom I referred had been stolen from-for over 50 years in some cases-and they set up an international cartel. We had to unite to fight it, but all it was was a group of producers making an agreement to get the price up to something equal to its competitive level measured against electricity, measured against the cost of producing oil from tar sands or whatever measure they used. We allowed ourselves as a nation-as the Europeans, the Americans and the Japanese did-to believe that when there is any evidence of a group of producers standing up to protect themselves by a price agreement, that must be fought, because if we had been stealing from them for 50 years that meant we had a God-given right to keep on stealing.
All this has been said, but it has to be said over and over again. There was no energy crisis in 1973. What there was, was a price adjustment going on. You do not bring out the troops when someone is finally getting a reasonably fair price for his product. Parliament acted fairly responsibly in 1973 and 1974 with respect to oil-it did in 1973, at least-when we said that we had to adjust, but by stages, and that we should try to adjust by keeping our prices just a little bit below the world price. All this was said by people of all parties in 1973. However, at the same time as oil prices started moving up, mineral prices also moved up. We have had a political record here for many years of asking the provinces to tax mines more heavily. Their tax level is a little lower than the average tax. Even royal commissions recommended that. Then suddenly when the provinces saw prices go up, they did exactly what we had been recommending; they raised their taxes on minerals
and on oil to get the windfall profit, which was theirs by right. They owned the property, but they had to break every agreement in the book to do it, which was immoral.
The faults we are discussing today are not entirely our own. It is a question of the greed of foreign governments. Our own governments have tried to grab as much as they could of this rising value of resources and, as a result, we have gone too far. The National Energy Program was based on an agreement with the provinces in which both levels of government tried to squeeze the most they could out of this resource. Legally and morally it all belonged to the provinces, but the provinces did not fight that issue. They simply fought to get the most they could, and the guy left at the bottom of the heap was, of course, the man who invested money in oil and gas companies. Of course, they had no choice but to move out, and they will not be coming back in for a little while. They had to move out because the moves we made gave a bigger percentage to the oil companies, but the percentage was of a much smaller pie. They still do not have any money.
We are paying a heavy price for ignoring the fundamentals of our Constitution and of what this Parliament is all about. We should be legislating here based on the Constitution, with a sense of equity and fairness; but we are overcome by this great greed on the parts of governments and all levels to get in on this bonanza of rising resource prices.
I say flatly that much of the blame is not only on our shoulders and the shoulders of the provinces and the companies but also on the shoulders of our courts. This is an unusual statement for a member of the Privy Council to make, but 1 honestly believe we in Parliament are going to have to face up to this issue and get our own thinking clear. If the courts cannot give us a decision according to what we meant in 1905, in 1930 and in 1867, I think we have a duty to propose a resolution stating flatly our interpretation of the legislation. As Your Honour knows, there are not too many precedents for that, but I think we may be forced into that because reality and common sense tell us that none of us is perfect. I would like to have Your Honour believe that what I have just said about the courts is reluctantly said, but I do say it. I have a feeling the courts have just as much frailty as we have and that until we make what we meant very clear in plain English, I think we will have to wait until we can get the courts to give decisions which are based on the real meaning of the legislators in 1867 and 1930.
I have already mentioned what should be done about this. I think we should have a resolution of both Houses putting into plain language what the property rights are and where they stand in relation to the trade power. We should take a look at property rights and where they stand in relation to prices. By juggling prices, can we pretend there is an emergency and change the Constitution? Can we relate property rights to the definition of crisis? These are things about which we will have to speak up if we want to clear our honour and reputation as parliamentarians.

My conclusion is on the political side. Much to the regret of all Canadians, there was a certain amount of politics involved in this whole issue. Originally it started out merely as an attack on Alberta, the "blue-eyed Arabs", and the people of Alberta responded, as we might expect, with pretty violent counter-attacks. Then this got down to realities in 1974 with the Petroleum Administration Act and became an attack on the oil producing provinces.
We had the federal government's response in 1974. All the provinces raised taxes on oil, gas and minerals, and the federal government came back with a sledge hammer response saying that all royalties and taxes of the provinces on oil and gas were non-deductible under federal income tax regulations. That was a complete breach of the Alberta Act and of the Saskatchewan Act of 1930, and a complete breach of the terms of Confederation in 1867. Many members of this House warned the government that an attack on one resource would lead to attacks on electric power in Ontario, Manitoba, B.C. and Quebec, and pretty soon in the Atlantic provinces. It soon moved into the forestry industry. Once the trend is set of the federal government, under very dubious constitutional authority, attacking the provinces, there is no end to it.
I think that in the next two years, and perhaps sooner, the Petroleum Administration Act should be subjected to a complete examination by the Supreme Court of Canada, particularly Clause 16 on page 11 of the bill which reads as follows:
Where no agreement is entered into under Section 22 with the government of a producer-province, or any such agreement is terminated by the declaration of the parties, or, in the opinion of the governor in council, is not effective or is not capable of being effective, the governor in council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude-
There is no other way to describe action where the federal government unilaterally takes the power to set prices for products that, under the Constitution, belong to that province, than to say it is stealing. Until the record is cleared of this provision which appears again, word for word, in the clause relating to gas, we in this House have not done our duty to the country.
There is nothing in these amendments that clarifies the principle of compensation. In the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta Acts of 1930, the principle of compensation is allowed if the federal government, for the national good, takes over any part of the property. That principle of compensation was vaguely included in the Petroleum Administration Act, but there was no clear-cut formula for it. The federal government can stake a claim to $50 billion or $60 billion worth of wealth for the next few years and the only compensation offered amounts to less than $2 billion. We have to face up to these things and get rid of the Petroleum Administration Act. Working in co-operation with the provinces is the only way to do that legally.
The final question that we have to ask is what we can do now that the bill is in place. I think the answer is self-evident. All this talk about how Alberta has backed up on the National Energy Program by $5 billion over the next five years, and the declaration that the federal government has backed up by $2
Petroleum Administration Act
billion, have not solved anything. Certainly this action has reduced the percentages taken by the province and the federal government. It has increased the percentage due to companies, although it has decreased the actual amount so that the companies have not been helped.
Where is the culprit then, Mr. Speaker? Over 80 per cent of the cost in any capital intensive enterprise today is accounted for by interest rates. A person who deals with small figures such as a $50,000 mortgage knows that over 30 years the mortgage will cost him $200,000. Based on 10 per cent money, over 75 per cent of the amount goes to interest.
What bothers the home owner is the same thing that bothers the oil companies. So much of the money they receive each year is spent on paying interest, and they do not have enough money left to pay back the principal. As a result there is a long period of pay-out. When they look at these figures and relate them to present value, they just drop all sorts of oil and gas projects. That applies to the mining industry as well-all sorts of minerals are left in the ground.
Under this method of financing, with long pay-out periods held up by high interest rates, every capital intensive project in the world is doomed, becuase this does not apply just in Canada. It applies to small people, to big people, to farmers and businessmen. There is no difference when it comes to fighting the common enemy.
Interest rates should be decided by the law of the market and not by the theoretical approach of a group of financial experts in world banking. We are part of a world system, so let it decide what interest rates shall be. With the present high interest rates in the United States and Canada, we are driven to Europe to get money at much lower interest rates. We all know where it comes from. The only risk is the fall of the dollar. These people, who have all this money to lend, are now proposing that if governments will borrow from them, they will lend it for a premium. It is just like buying insurance-it protects the borrower and the lender both. If the premium is less than two per cent and the money is borrowed at six to nine the per cent, it is not a bad deal.
I think we should get our house in order and make a deal with the provinces and the oil companies that everyone will get off the back of the industry, and that the industry will not take anything out either, until the debt is paid back. There is hardly an oil field or gas field that I know of, or a combination field, that could not pay back in four to five years at present prices. Once free of the interest load, and the principal load, there would be a big pie to be divided. Under a contractual arrangement all that would be necessary would be to decide how it should be divided.
All these matters were discussed in great detail when the Hon. Donald Macdonald was minister of energy, mines and resources, and when the Hon. John Turner was minister of finance. Both gentlemen are on the public record of this House as agreeing that this is the right way to go about things. The companies would have enough operating capital and also would make a good profit. Mr. Macdonald suggested that the

There is no need to panic. We have had interest rates bothering us for over 3,000 years. Look back at the laws of Greece and Rome. All their major reforms had to do with interest rates. It is not a new problem. In 1919 there was a great uproar in western Canada and Ontario about high interest rates. The farmers threw out the other parties, elected a new party called the Progressives, and scared the daylights out of the government of the day.
We then got an amendment to the Bank Act which put a ceiling on interest rates of 6 per cent. The banks operated for years under that ceiling, and grew and prospered. Now we have changed that.
The banks came in with a very good argument, based on a royal commission report, that if we took off that ceiling they would compete so hard that interest rates would go down, perhaps to 3 per cent or 4 per cent. Well, Parliament bought that argument. But we had not figured on theoreticians saying that high interest rates were good for our souls, and we would have to slow down our growth because we were too greedy and enjoying life too much. They have us slowed down all right, but they are ruining us in the process.
The amendments contained in motion Nos. 4 and 5, Mr. Speaker, say in substance that we should, in our own interests, reduce taxes. But more basic even than the reduction of taxes is that there should be a recognition that there is a lot more to do. I would like to see come out of this debate recognition of that fact by all parties. In the meantime we can show our sincerity, and concern over where we are going, by supporting these two motions.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to follow the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). For a relative novice like myself it is very stimulating to hear the hon. member bring forward a great deal of argument of historical relevance to some of the discussions we have in the House. I think the basic point the hon. member referred to is indeed a question that Canadians must be pondering as they listen to debates like this, read the newspapers, and note the progress of events in Canada over the past months, indeed years.
The question the hon. member raised and responded to was really whether legislation like Bill C-103 has been brought in knowingly and purposely by a government with a particular
direction and motive to be served. I, like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, do not know the answer for sure. What I do know is that many of the measures brought in during the time I have been able to follow politics closely all have a common thread. Through the 1970s right up till now we have seen progressively greater government involvement through legislation in the fields of health care, energy, and business. Maybe that is by accident, but I think we have to question this seriously, as previous speakers have done today.
As I speak on these two motions, Mr. Speaker, I am going to make a specific proposal. I shall not ask for much, but I would like to have the opportunity to suggest to the Minister of Energy (Mr. Lalonde)-who is in the House and I hope will be here when I make the proposal-that we make one change which I believe will help to overcome some of the difficulties created by the NEP. I will get to that specific suggestion in a few moments.
Motion No. 4 was presented for a very specific reason, and people might wonder why we suggested $28 as a possible increase in that motion. The $28 translates into what amounts to an 18-cents a gallon tax. As it stands now, the tax would be $78 a cubic metre of oil, or 48 cents a gallon. The tax is now about 24 cents a gallon and it will rise to 48 cents under the authority of this legislation. We chose that figure of $28 because we have seen over the past few years, the NEP, the minister, indeed the whole government being very seriously compromised in the eyes of the Canadian people.
We have seen how the 18-cent a gallon tax was dealt with by the government when it was in opposition and during the last federal election, and it is in Motion No. 4 to show the Canadian people in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, in fact in the minister's own province of Quebec, that there is a very serious question about the legitimacy of introducing additional taxation. This bill amounts to taxation without representation because it will allow the minister, in his own way and in his own time, without any additional review, to increase those taxes significantly.
At a time when Canadians had been living with energy prices that were well out of line with world energy prices we were faced with a serious political problem, because it was pretty difficult to run a campaign telling people that they should pay more for energy. That is difficult enough, but the hard part is to do that when you have other people in the same campaign telling people that they do not have to pay more, indeed should not pay more because it would not be fair or equitable and "if you voted in a particular way, you would not have to face that kind of increase."
Memories are short. Sometimes it serves a purpose to forget things that happened years ago, but two and a half years are not that long ago. In that two and a half years we have had successive increases in energy prices which make a mockery out of the claims and promises made to the Canadian people at that time. They may have been justified if there was some way

At the time we faced the challenge of having to defend increased energy prices we knew there was a considerable amount of criticism attached to the fact that we suggested energy prices should increase by 18 cents. What were we hoping to gain by that 18-cent increase? First, we could have avoided some of the confrontation with the producing provinces. More important we were looking at a way to bring Canadian energy self-sufficiency and energy security into focus so that by 1990 Canada, as a nation, would not have to depend on unstable and unreliable sources of oil and petroleum products from other parts of the world. Considerable blame was attached to our party for trying to do that. It is somewhat reminiscent of the position the government has now, of attaching blame to other people for the economic crisis in Canada.
It has been a long time since we have heard the government take responsibility for interest rates and the kind of financial policy that we have in our country. Right now we are told that it is the fault of the United States because of its interest rate policy, and that it does not really matter that our interest rates are several points higher than those in the United States. Obviously if you can make the political argument that it is not your fault, that is the best political position you can have. But if Canadians and the Canadian government are not to blame for the kind of economic policy that we have, who is to blame?
The Americans do not make our laws. The Americans have not been in charge of our economic policy for the last 14 years. The Americans have not been in charge of legislation that has controlled energy development in Canada for the past 14 years. The Americans do not determine what the Governor of the Bank of Canada does.
This government continually uses scapegoats. The Government blames the opposition for creating unrest in the Canadian people because it says we talk of things that hurt people, about people losing their homes, their farms and their businesses. Similarly the government has blamed OPEC for setting prices for petroleum products higher and higher. The government blames the United States government because of its domestic interest rate policy. This government continually avoids its responsibility for the programs it has put in place over the last 14 years. The taxes that have been put on petroleum products in Canada are taxes on top of other taxes. But now I think this government is in danger of the Canadian

people reacting. It will be a reaction that has never been experienced by any other government in Canada before.
What I am speaking of has happened south of the border. What happened in California is an example of this. Several days ago I put a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in this House. I suggested to him that one of the major reasons for a decline in domestic oil requirements was the recession. He quickly responded we did not have a recession at all last year. In fact, he said that our gross national product increased by 3 per cent. That response, I think, points out a very real problem, and it is partly responsible for the introduction of Motion No. 5 by our party.
I think the minister should look at the last six months of 1981 and he will find gross domestic expenditure decreased in the third quarter by minus 0.5 per cent and it decreased in the fourth quarter by minus 0.9 per cent. Therefore, in the last six months of 1981 Canada started to experience a serious and a significant recession. Authorities are now saying that if things continue with the same single mindedness which the Minister of Energy and others have expressed over the last several months, we will be facing an economic situation which will be truly classed as a depression. But from what we have seen so far from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Energy it will be six months or even a year after that before they will even know it has happened.
That is one of the problems of this government. I do not know whether its members think a thing will go away if they first deny it and then blame it on someone else. After that we have to hope there will be some kind of a response. But the question is whether we will get a response that will make a significant difference or whether we will get band-aid measures, in other words, whether we will get an aspirin or the cure. We had an example with the changes to the National Energy Program called "Update 1982." These changes were put into a very pretty red document. The update contains a lot of information. The taxes which are being presented to Canadians require some explanation. Most of us would accept the fact that the federal government needs revenue or needs somehow to raise money, because it provides some programs which are of benefit. There are criticisms which can be made of many of the programs, but I think the need for revenue is understood.

The important point is that of this increase, $409, or nearly 80 per cent, was paid indirectly to the federal government. About one third of the total taxes are federal taxes. This massive increase has created many difficulties, whether in terms of heating homes, operating farms, or operating businesses. The massive increase varies, but 80 per cent of it can be related to federal taxes.
With Motion No. 4 we have tried to put a limit on how much the federal government can take from the pockets of Canadians. We have tried to keep the hand of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources out of the pockets of Canadian businessmen, Canadian farmers, and Canadian home owners who have to heat with oil because alternatives are unavailable to them, and there are still a good many such home owners.
Our second motion is designed to try to put some control on the petroleum compensation charge. The charge in this year alone resulted in revenues being taken in that were $1.4 billion in excess of what was required. This really amplifies one of the points I tried to make earlier, that the indirect response or lack of sensitivity to a changing environment, of the federal government, whether it be a departmental problem or a question of not understanding quickly what is going on, resulted in this additional amount being taken directly out of the pockets of consumers when it was not justified in the legislation we have, and not for the purposes for which it was designed.
We have an extra $1.4 billion which has been taken as a compensation charge on energy which must be imported from offshore. That money, which will be used by the federal government to avoid consumer reaction in Canada when prices would have risen in July, has been sitting there and gradually increasing over the past year because the federal government did not have the ability to respond quickly to a changing scene. The original justification given for this charge was to pay for
June 7, 1982

oil imports. It has now collected SI.4 billion more than it needs.
There are several ways to approach the current situation. Through our motion we have attempted to ensure that it be the government's responsibility to prevent an exorbitant amount of money being collected in an unfair or unreasonable manner. A number of other steps could be taken, particularly with respect to resources of that magnitude. I would like to propose a concept to the minister which I hope he will at least consider. It is a positive suggestion which may help him, particularly in the face of his many failures over the past several years. It may be a way to help him to achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990, which we would all like to see, and it may help rationalize some of the inequities which exist in Canada's energy scene.
The hon. member who spoke just prior to me suggested as well that Canada had many forms of energy running out of its ears. It is a known fact that we are net exporters of energy. We also know that there are many arbitrary and unrealistic pieces of legislation and policies regarding various forms of energy. For example, electricity is treated differently from oil. Solar energy is treated differently from other types of energy. Various forms of energy are not considered for their respective values but only when they happen to evolve through various forms of development.
This taxation measure, which has resulted in federal coffers being swollen by $1.4 billion more than is needed, presents an opportunity to introduce a concept of parity in the various energy fields. This may not be a new concept, since I know that the minister realizes that a calorie is a calorie is a calorie. However, as far as I can determine there is very little legislation to show that we are making any serious attempt to address the issue of equally developing different forms of energy.
I believe it is important to realize that while many people are looking at the husbanding of the petroleum industry and its resources, which we know are finite, we now have an opportunity to enter some of the windows of technology and to take advantage of some new opportunities for energy resources which have been developed to the point where commercialization is possible. A possible alternative manner in which this petroleum compensation charge to equalize the difference between domestic and imported oil could be used is to use a small portion of the fund to provide a balance which would allow other energy sources to be developed to the point of competetiveness, and enter through the window where these resources can be expanded at a pace which the marketplace would allow.
Let us use solar energy as an example. We know that each barrel of oil has approximately four gigajoules of energy. An equivalent value of gigajoule solar energy could be determined considering the world price, domestic price and the import compensation charge. On a comparison basis solar hot water heating would cost $100 per gigajoule.
This is what the compensation charge gives in a preferential way to the Canadian energy scene in order to pay for the difference between domestic and imported oil. Why can we not
Petroleum Administration Act
introduce the concept of parity and allow that level of compensation to an energy source which would replace a given amount of oil with an equivalent amount of alternate energy? It would be an equalizer in the system and would help develop a source of energy which is at a commercial stage now, and which can reliably provide 50 per cent of our hot water needs in the domestic situation, and probably a lot more in some commercial operations. This would allow it to earn its way. It would amount to $100 per gigajoule. Although these figures could be refined, I am confident that this is approximately what it would cost. It could be worked out under a grants system or other financing programs. The equalizer would be $100 per gigajoule, which is roughly equivalent to $400 per barrel over a 20-year period. This is one manner of relating different types of energy on an equal and even basis.
The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), who will speak after me, will have more to say about the tar sands issue. I am not suggesting that we extend the use of solar energy, which includes ethanol and methanol to the point where we no longer need the tar sands or Cold Lake, but only to the point where it is on equal footing with those petroleum resources. If we relate the amount of spending to stimulate the industry in the Alsands project, to another energy area one can see a significant opportunity to provide the energy which we are missing since it is presently unavailable.
Everyone knows that those projects must and will be developed at the appropriate time, but it probably will not happen until a change in government. However, at this point there are many things which can be done to help provide a replacement for the loss of security and oil production which would have come from those projects. I would appreciate it if the minister would consider that suggestion. We will be presenting an additional amendment to suggest precisely that.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for the opportunity to speak on Bill C-103 and the motions to amend it, Motions Nos. 4 and 5 which we are presently discussing. Motion No. 4 states:
That Bill C-103, an act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be amended in Clause 31 by striking out line 13 at page 19 and substituting the following therefor:-
We should remember that on page 19 the words that our party wants to strike out are the words "amount not exceeding seventy-five dollars", and we want to substitute the words "amount not exceeding twenty-eight dollars".
The change proposed here would lower the maximum level of the petroleum compensation charge to $28 per cubic metre from the $75 set down in the bill as it now reads. The petroleum compensation charge is presently levied at a rate of $39.64 per cubic metre, or $6.30 per barrel, which has the effect of raising gasoline prices at the pump by 24 cents per gallon.
In effect, this amendment would force the government to lower the petroleum compensation charge from its present

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
level and require that the excess amounts collected by the petroleum compensation charge at the rate above $28 per cubic metre since January, 1981, be reimbursed to Canadians through a lowering of the petroleum compensation charge. The $28 per cubic metre, approximately $4.50 per barrel, would limit the PCC effect upon motor gasoline prices to 18 cents per gallon. I think that might sound vaguely familiar. This is the same increase, of course, as was proposed in the Crosbie budget-
Pure coincidence.

-and which has more than doubled under the Liberals since December, 1979.
The petroleum compensation charge has been the largest component in the Liberal-caused gasoline price increases, having been raised from a level which translates from four cents a gallon at the pumps to 24 cents per gallon.
The government ended up with a surplus in the petroleum compensation fund last year, 1981, of $1.4 billion. Where is the $1.4 billion? Is it in general revenue? Is it another form of taxation? This is a far cry from what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) acknowledges may be a slight surplus.
It is a reasonable amendment and one which I feel the government should seriously consider. Motion No. 5 which, again, is a conservation motion, would add the following:
The tariff of charges set out under subsection (1.1) shall be set at such a level that the aggregate of revenues from those charges does not exceed the amount required to pay the compensation payable under the provisions of Division I of this act.
In other words, what we are basically saying is that there should be a sliding scale for the compensation charge. Surely the monitoring board can determine what the compensation charge should be. Surely the monitoring board can monitor the price of oil that we must purchase from off shore and compensate it accordingly so that Canadians are not overtaxed for this compensation fund. If we added this new subsection to the Petroleum Administration Act, it would write into law the rules for setting the charge that is now only implied by the way the scheme is supposed to operate.
It would require the petroleum compensation board to monitor any changes in the cost of imports so as to be able to make the appropriate changes in the petroleum compensation charges as quickly as possible. In other words, we would not then go through what we did over the past eight months when we found we were in the ludicrous situation of importing oil from other countries. At that time, the refiners were able to purchase on the spot market more cheaply, by up to $4 a barrel, because the compensation charge was paid, which effectively shut in crude oil in the western basin. We were importing oil and it was being paid by the taxpayer, the guy who pulled up to the pump to fill his tank. The petroleum compensation charge was actually being used to give windfall profits to the refiners in Montreal. I cannot imagine anything more idiotic or stupid.
As I said before, in 1981 there was a surplus of more than $1.4 billion from taxes to raise revenues for the purpose of subsidizing oil imports. Obviously, the level of charges should have been adjusted and should be adjusted in the future to raise only enough revenue to cover the cost of subsidizing imports. An error of $ 1.4 billion, as I said before, is definitely more than the small surplus which is possible according to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I am sorry to see the minister leave.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I'm listening to you.

One thing has become very apparent to me since coming to this House. I suppose it has been partially due to my background in a small business, not a large business. However, I think it also holds true with large businesses, or in the business community in general, that when a mistake is made in a business decision, the people responsible for running that business admit their mistake. They admit it immediately and say, "It is wrong and we have to correct it".
It was very obvious that when the government introduced its tax measure in the guise of a national energy policy, a mistake was made. The government insists on going along the same road with that mistake, instead of standing up and saying, "We made a mistake. We will have to re-evaluate. We will have to change". But, no, we do not hear that. If the government admitted its mistake, I would be the first one to stand in this House and say, "Good for you. You recognized the mistake and you will change it". But instead, we stand here, discussing over and over again the problems that the national energy policy has created for my constituency, for the Alberta and Saskatchewan economies, and, indeed, for the Ontario and Quebec economies. It has affected virtually every province in this great country of ours.
However, these discussions fall on deaf ears. Why? It is because hon. members come to this House, and they can only think to themselves, "We cannot show that we are backing down. The government never makes mistakes." That is absolute, total garbage, and any reasonable man will understand that governments make mistakes as businesses make mistakes, and as individuals make mistakes. However, it takes courage, it takes leadership, and it takes vision to be able to stand up and say, "We have made the mistake and we will rectify it." We do not find that courage in the present government. We do not find it in the cabinet. We do not find it in the back benches. In the government we do not find the leadership which has the vision to see what it is doing to the country. I spend a great deal of time talking to members on the opposite side, both cabinet members and backbenchers. Individually, I find them to be thoughtful, considerate, capable men. As a group, with policy set by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who has lost all sense of direction, they lose all this. They lose it the minute they walk into this House and legislation is introduced.
In committee we go through legislation clause by clause. I have had Liberal backbenchers come to me after sitting on the national energy committee and saying that what the national
June 7, 1982

energy policy is doing to the oil industry in this country is a crime. They do not have the courage to say that in committee or to stand up and say it in the House.
Name them.
I find that absolutely sickening.
Do you have the courage to name them?
I suggest that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) talk to some of those members.
Which ones? Who are they?

The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) brought in an update on his energy policy. He will give back more than $2 billion. I say give back because the national energy policy is not an energy policy but a tax policy. It is a tax policy of greed of this government which wants money to allow it to continue spending like a drunken sailor all across this country.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is marching backward to the tune of $2.5 billion. Something must be wrong. However, that is the only time Canada starts to march forward. I would say that is not enough. The investment climate in this country today has been totally destroyed. Investors will not invest in Canada. Why should they trust a government which moves in with a national energy policy by which it steals 25 per cent of the assets that have been developed? It does that through a back-in provision of the national energy policy. It is not just foreign investors but Canadian investors as well who do not want to invest in the economy of Canada. They do not look forward to the time when things are going to change.
I travel around my riding talking to businessmen and entrepreneurs. They believed that this country had a future and wanted to invest in it. They wanted to build something from nothing. They wanted to build something by themselves. I talk to these people no more. They are bailing out as fast as they can, those who are still surviving, those who have not gone bankrupt or are in receivereship.
These people are putting their money into cash investments in order to draw interest. Why work 16 or 18 hours a day for a government that is greedy? The government will either heavily tax those people or, with the stroke of a pen on one fateful night in the House, change the economic climate with a budget called the national energy policy.
The only problem with the oil industry today is government greed. The oil industry was making the wheels of the Canadian economy spin, creating jobs right across this country. What did the government do? It attacked the multinationals. It said that "multinational" was a good dirty word and it could use it to swing Canadians behind the government. It was not the multinationals that got hurt. It was those Canadians who were doing exactly what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources wanted them to do, those Canadians who, as statistics will show, were buying the oil industry. He said it is dong what the government said it would do. He says, "Look how we are conserving oil in Canada, thousands of barrels a day." He says, "We are using less than we were last year or before the introduction of the national energy policy."
That is because the wheels of industry have ground to a halt. Plants are closing in Ontario and Quebec. Oil rigs, service rigs and trucks in western Canada are being sold. Two men in Fort McMurray built one of the finest welding and machine shops north of the city of Edmonton to service the industry. Then the national energy policy came in and everything these men had built up over 20 or 25 years went down the tube. I talked to the wife of one of these gentlemen. They had lost their home and their furniture. The sheriff stood in the doorway and told them to take only their personal belongings. She asked me whether there was anything I could do. The sheriff would not let her take a table that belonged to her great-grandmother. I could do nothing because it was classed as household furniture. In spite of this, the minister congratulates himself on the success of his national energy policy.
We were told that after the energy agreement was signed, Alsands and the Cold Lake synthetic oil plants would go ahead. As we all know, they died. We were told that the energy agreement would encourage Alberta's petrochemical industry. Now the economic development minister for Alberta has stated that the Ottawa domestic tax on ethane threatens to make Alberta non-competitive. That is strictly a federal tax imposed by a greedy government, with no thought to what it is doing to the industry. Or, if there is a thought, it is a designed thought, and I do not believe that anyone could be that callous and say, "We are going to teach Alberta, we are going to teach these people in the west a lesson." I do not believe it. I believe it is ignorance on the minister's part. He is listening to bureaucrats who do not understand what they have done.
