The national energy policy was imposed on western Canada by a government without representation in the west. It was imposed on the energy industry without any representation or discussion with that industry. The national energy policy seeks to control Canadian economy, with bureaucratic control and government control. This is the government that rewards people like Branny Schepanovich with a directorship on Air Canada. He is the Liberal in Alberta, the one and only Liberal in Alberta, who is supposed to be the superman in the organization field. He has been a Liberal since he left university about 16 or 20 years ago. He has let his neck stick out there. He has received his just reward, on the board of directors of Air Canada. That is the sickness of this government.
There is a survey just released from the Petroleum Services Association. 1 would like to put it on the record for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He has left the House again but perhaps his parliamentary secretary could bring it to his attention. He will not believe it, he will think up some reason why this cannot be, because it is coming from an opposition member. I ask him to get a copy of it. Let us look at this survey. It is a survey by the Petroleum Services Association. It says that 13 oil-well drilling and service companies have gone bankrupt, and that 23 more oil-well drilling and servicing companies are expected to go bankrupt this year. Where are they located? They are all located in Alberta and Saskatchewan. And 12,000 direct jobs have been lost in that area of the oil industry since the national energy policy, that is direct jobs, and I stress direct, because it is too difficult to determine how many indirect jobs are lost, because they are not buying pipe, they are not buying trucks, they are not buying motors. We all know where those materials are produced. They say that 227 drilling rigs have left Canada, rigs that were busy in Canada and working in Canada. Those 227 drilling rigs have left Canada since the inception of the national energy policy.
What is a drilling rig? Let us talk about that, Mr. Speaker. It consists of 227 small factories employing anywhere from 24 to 35 or 40 people. It is a small factory on its own. Can you imagine the hue and cry that would come out of Quebec or Ontario if 227 small factories were forced to close the door because the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) introduced that policy into the House of Commons and at one stroke of the pen destroyed this industry? Can you imagine that? But we cry in the wilderness in the hinterland provinces, and it upsets me. Members will get up and say that it is members from the other
side of the House, members who go back to their riding, who are causing the division in our land. That is not true and they know full well that it is not true. We have 461 drilling rigs left in Canada today. Of those 461 that are not being put up for auction-some of them will be, they will be going across the auction block soon-out of those 461 drillings rigs there are 84 actually drilling in the western basin today.
What about the downturn in the economy? If they were receiving for their production the world price, the same price that we pay Venezuela or Mexico or Iran or Saudi Arabia, if they were allowed to go in and drill without the tax regime that is being placed in front of them now, they would be finding the oil. But the attack was on. I am convinced that the attack was on the western basin. It was an attack on the oil industry in general, it was an attack that said, "We are going to move all the focus on energy development and finding the oil; we are going to move it to Canada lands, to the north, to the offshore." Even with the collapse of Alsands and the shelving of the Cold Lake project, we still hear the minister saying that the Alsands are not needed, that we will have plenty of oil coming from the Beaufort Sea in the north, that we will still have plenty of oil over in Hibernia. Mr. Speaker, they think they had it tough with Alberta when they were trying to work out an equitable agreement on sharing the exploitation of the natural resources in Alberta. "They ain't seen nuthin' yet" because I do not think Newfoundlanders will stand by and allow this government to steamroll over them, not for one minute. I am absolutely 100 per cent behind the Newfoundland government. This government knows nothing but unilateral action. That was confirmed when this government said the reserves in the Hibernia field and off the coast of Newfoundland belong to the federal government. The federal government has been unable to negotiate because it does not sit down and talk and try to work things out in a co-operative way, in the old way, in the Canadian way. Hon. members opposite emulate our famous Prime Minister, who stood and said, "Co-operative federalism is dead". In other words, "To hell with the provinces, we will do it our way or it will not be done". Where are those members of the Liberal Party who sit in government? Where are those backbenchers with spines who can stand up and tell their leader that enough is enough because what he is doing is destroying Canada?
I have never seen more animosity toward a government on the part of the people generally than I have seen build up over the past two years. That scares me because I love my country. I want my country to become great. I want my country to adopt the vision adopted by people like Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We have lost that vision totally because of one man and his lackeys in the cabinet.
I have said it before and I will say it again: only ten backbench Liberal members are needed to stand and say to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, "Enough is enough". They are destroying the
June 7, 1982

country, and if they will not admit their mistakes, those ten backbench Liberal members could withdraw their support. That would change the direction of this country.
People in this country no longer have any faith that things will turn around. I had occasion to speak with a chap who had been down in the United States, where the rate of unemployment is high. He was down there on business for a week. He told me he got a real boost when he went down there because the attitude of the man on the street-the people-is that they will work together and beat this thing. Their attitude is that they will drive inflation down, as they are doing. Their attitude is that they will drive interest rates down and get their country moving again. There are problems in the United States, but that chap told me that coming to Canada is like coming to another world. Businessmen are down. They are looking for more of the same that we have seen over the past two years. They are asking us when we will get rid of our incompetent government, which is doing nothing. There is indecision. There is no longer any national will in Canada. It is gone. It is gone because of the divisive, unilateral policies of the present government. I never thought I would see the day when individual Canadians would hang their heads and say, "I don't see a future here." Men I have known intimately since I was in grade school have telephoned me and approached me to ask if I could find out how they could emigrate to the United States or Australia. At least ten have done that, and that is a conservative estimate. There are men who love their country but no longer see a future here because of this continuing idiocy.
The amendments we have moved are very reasonable. All we are asking is that the government stop ripping off the people at the pumps through its National Energy Program. If the government needs a petroleum compensation charge, sure, Canadians do not mind spreading the grief around and compensating those in other parts of the country who have to pay more for gas or fuel. But why should the minister be allowed to gather up in his kitty $1.4 billion, as he did last year, and then say, "Well, there might be a slight increase?" Our amendments are reasonable amendments. They should be looked at, and I hope the government will act on them.
With that, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you very much. I appreciate the time you have given to me.

Mr. Speaker, 1 follow the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) with some sadness. 1 know him to be a very forthright man who is deeply concerned about his country. I sat here for 35 minutes and listened to the impassioned plea of a representative of a great part of Canada which is, of course, the oil sands centre. What is perhaps even more important, the hon. member for Athabasca is a man who thoroughly understands the industry and thoroughly understands the arduous task of making a living under the uncertain conditions this government has imposed not only on him but also on the men, women and families he represents.
It was disquieting to hear the hon. member for Athabasca talk about the loss of oil drilling rigs and the loss of jobs, not just in Alberta but right across the country. As the hon. member pointed out, we know where pumps are built. We
Petroleum Administration Act
know where pipes are put together. We know where gaskets are made. We know where trucks are manufactured. Indeed, we know where refrigerators, toasters and irons are manufactured. As the hon. member for Athabasca has said, it is not just the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan who are affected.
What bothered me most was the hon. member's despair and his near loss of hope. That is what we must redress, and there must be changes.
Under the leadership of our distinguished energy critic, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), we have put forward a number of amendments. There are more with which we must yet deal. We have put forward amendments attempting to remove, for example, Clause 12. Such amendments would, in effect, do away completely with the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge. We have dealt with that. That motion is pending and will be voted upon in due course. It attempts to bring some sense to the direction in which this government is leading us with the support of the National Energy Program.
In our second motion, which has already been discussed, we have attempted to restore some direction as well. In that instance we did so by moving to strike out Clause 16 for the purpose of denying the cabinet the unilateral power to revoke price agreements. This afternoon the hon. member for Calgary Centre spoke at some length about the government's attitude to written contracts. It was a damning comment on the government's regard for agreements.
In our third motion we approach the question of credibility and attempt to restore some rational approach to it. This is a reasonably technical amendment which deals with bringing into balance the pricing of crude oil, which will affect those who do the exploration and consumers who use the product as well as governments.
The motion before the House now extends that attempt to bring some sanity and some thoughtful rationale into the process. The change proposed would have the effect of lowering the maximum level of the petroleum compensation charge to some $28 per cubic metre from the $75 provided in the bill as it stands.
The PCC is presently levied at the rate of $39.64 per cubic metre or about $6.30 per barrel. This has the effect of raising the price of gasoline at the pump by 24 cents per gallon. Our amendment would force the government to lower the PPC from its present level and require that the excess collected above the $28 per cubic metre since January, 1981 be reimbursed to Canadians, through lowering the PCC.
In actual fact, as has been pointed out by others on this side of the House, this is more than symbolic; in a sense it is poetic. It would have the effect of limiting government to its promises of just a couple of years ago. It would also have the effect of reducing the increase in the cost of gasoline to the 18 cents per gallon level promised by the hon. member for St. John's West

The need for these approaches becomes clear in other amendments. There is a need for guidelines that are understandable, credible, believeable, workable and acceptable. Our next amendment would achieve those things. We would require monitoring and adjustments from guidelines that would be understandable, that would be known and would be clear. If we had a projection of the money that will be collected by the government if left untethered, it would be revealing. The hon. member for Athabasca and others have touched on this in recent months. We all know that we could do better on the spot market.
It is pleasant to see that the distinguished Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) from Halifax has entered the House. I trust he raises his voice in caucus-
He does.

Not to much effect, though. I would put this rhetorical question to him: who pays the second highest electricity rates in the country south of 60 and north of 45? Was he effective with his colleagues on that one?

speechtext: How much higher would they be if we had gone to world price for oil?

We would be at 18 cents per gallon instead of 92! I do not have to calculate that for the minister.
There would be no need for massive increases in the cost of electricity in the Atlantic provinces next year if the minister had shown any concern and had approached the government asking it for compassion to include some cushion for people on fixed and low incomes in its program.
Prince Edward Island is paying two and a half times the domestic electricity rate of any other place in southern Canada, from P.E.I. to Vancouver. From north of 45 and south of 55, no one is paying more than Prince Edward Islanders. Very few people pay more than Newfoundlanders and even fewer pay more than Nova Scotians where the cost of electricity is approaching twice the national average: In part, that is because the petroleum compensation charges are so far in excess of reality that they have driven the price of oil-fired electricity way up.
The distinguished member from Halifax may speak out in caucus and cabinet, but he does not speak out in public very often. He has not been effective because the cost of electricity in Nova Scotia is double, and in some cases is more than double, the cost to other Canadians.
There is a great need for a return to some semblance of reality, and this can be seen in a number of ways. As the oil compensation charge now stands, it hurts farmers, fishermen and those who must find their living in our forests, as well as
small industry. It is not just the domestic users of electricity who are affected; the entire secondary manufacturing base is directly affected at a time when it is difficult enough for them to survive the present high interest rates and bad mortgages. It affects our fishermen, and it affects our young people who might very well want to go into fishing or follow their parents on the farm. It is discouraging because there is no end to it. The effect of our amendment would be to take away the excess amount of taxation and allow people a little bit of freedom and a greater opportunity to get on with the development of their own lives.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, as we will be demonstrating in the days ahead, we want to put some sunset clauses into this bill with respect to the charges. We will move amendments which stipulate that the charge will continue only until it has reached $1.46 billion, that being the amount required to buy Petrofina, not including the brokerage fees paid to-the minister's son is with us today in the gallery, Mr. Speaker. Happy birthday. How is he going to get a job? Ask Dave that tonight. Today is a very significant day for David Regan; he becomes a teenager today. His dad is a better fighter than that; he is a better fighter for all Canadians. We look forward to great things from him in the area of oil and gas pricing.
We will move other amendments in this area, Mr. Speaker, which we hope will have the impact of ensuring that the Canadian ownership account is used for its original purpose: to increase Canadian ownership. There is nothing complex about that. As it now reads, the bill allows the government to buy Canadian companies; that is not increasing Canadian ownership. The whole purpose of the Canadian ownership account and these enormously inflated tax levels was to increase Canadian ownership. You do not increase Canadian ownership by buying companies already Canadian owned. At least if you do, I have not quite been able to figure out how. Perhaps someone over there might enlighten us. The points we are putting forward have been designed to try to rationalize this process and return some sanity to the NEP.
The hon. member for Athabasca said that individually members over there are not bad; some of them are reasonably intelligent. The whip is a great man but apparently unable to persuade his colleagues to a sensible point of view. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) is unable to persuade anyone. On his own he is not a bad fellow; reasonably intelligent, smiles once in awhile. Too bad he does not have a military force to play with any more. As you go down the line, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc), on their own, after five in the afternoon, are not bad fellows. But something happens to them when they go to work at 8.30 in the morning, and no one has been able to quite figure out what it is.
Three or four times today, directly and indirectly, the Acting Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin),
June 7, 1982

was asked: have you talked to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)? Well, do you know what I believe? Since the Prime Minister went to Versailles, not one of them has picked up the phone and called the leader of this country and said, "Look, we have a problem. What are you doing over there? What are we supposed to say to Canadians?" Mr. Speaker, I do not think there has been any communication whatsoever. Is that the way you operate? Is that what happens to you between 8.30 in the morning and when you leave your office? Do you lose all capacity to communicate with one another except through the bureaucracy? Perhaps if you did talk to each other, the time of the House would not be taken up trying to restore some sanity to the minister's NEP.
All we are trying to do, Mr. Speaker, is to take the excess taxes-which in some cases have been misused or ill used, improperly used certainly-and put them back into the pockets of Canadians. We want to give the little fellow a break, the senior citizens, persons on fixed incomes or low pensions. Give the fellow driving a car a bit of a break. For most Canadians a car is no longer a luxury, it is a matter of necessity. That is what we are trying to do, curb the over-zealousness and blindness of this government in its pursuit of an energy program which has failed this country. They were warned it would fail, and yet they steadfastly and blindly refused to alter or change it.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this debate will carry on. The debate in the country will carry on. Sooner or later, whether or not it is here on the floor of this chamber, the answers to these questions will be given. The questions will be answered in a general federal election. If one were held tomorrow the questions would be answered to the very clear and distinct advantage of the Canadians who have to bear the very unfair burden of this government's National Energy Program. Somebody said the other day that if you cannot talk to one another any more, that if you are so broken down in the treasury benches that no longer are there lines of communication, that if you do not hear direction from the Prime Minister as to what you should be doing here, and if you have lost control of the bureaucracy-the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is one sign of that and the National Energy Program of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is a clear indication of it-why in the name of all that is good and holy do you not do the honourable thing, call a general election and resign?

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to speak on report stage of Bill C-103 and the two motions before us tonight. I, like many members, have had the opportunity to speak at some length on second reading of this bill. At that time I laid before the House those things that I thought objectionable in the bill, the philosophies contained therein and the principles which were incorporated in it. In reading the draft which has emerged from committee I do not think many improvements have been made. It is my intention tonight to impose upon myself the rules of relevancy. These are not usually adhered to strictly in the House. But I intend to speak solely on the proposals that came out of the
Petroleum Administration Act
Standing Committee on Energy Legislation and the two motions before us tonight. As a consequence, my presentation will likely be rather technical, somewhat dry but, mercifully, quite short.
It seems the changes proposed at report stage by and large are technical changes. There has been no change in policy and no change in substance. We are dealing with rather small technical changes. I wish that had not been so, but what more can you expect from the government in office?
I count about five separate proposals in the bill reported to this House on June 1 by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette). In my opinion, it proved to be somewhat of a disappointment. The first change is to be incorporated into Clause 9 and Clause 33 of the bill. Clause 9 deals with penalties for the non-payment of the oil export charge, Clause 33 deals with very similar penalties to be levied for non-payment of the petroleum compensation charge. I point out that the penalties referred to here are not penalties to be imposed in the case of fraud; they are penalties such as those with which the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) is familiar. They are not cases of deliberate fraud but rather oversights on the part of people supposed to be paying these taxes.
In the original Petroleum Administration Act, the amount of penalty to be levied in cases of default was 1 per cent of the outstanding amount. This seemed quite fair and reasonable. People have lived with that levy for some time and have become used to it. However, in the original version of Bill C-103 it was the intention of the government to increase this penalty charge from 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent of the outstanding balance. I do not know why the government wanted to increase it by that amount. It would seem that 1 per cent per month, which is 14 per cent or 15 per cent per annum, is quite reasonable when there is no case of deliberate fraud. I presume the government thought that inflation would continue and in that case it might be better to levy a penalty charge amounting to some 20 per cent per annum or 1.5 per cent per month.
I am pleased to see that the penalty was rolled back to the original amount prescribed under the Petroleum Administration Act, that is, 1 per cent. In effect, having gone through this exercise, there is no change. I am pleased to support this recommendation of the committee, and I do not think any useful purpose was served by the proposed increase to 1.5 per cent per month.
I would, however, point out that when it comes to deliberate non-payment of the various charges and taxes to be levied, then we have a much different situation. The government has in no way backed down from the vicious penalties that it wishes to impose on people for deliberate non-payment. As an example, I will quote from page 12 of the bill. Clause 18 refers to penalties to be levied with respect to non-payment of the transportation fuel recovery compensation charge. These are very similar penalties prescribed for the non-payment of the compensation charge or non-payment of the oil export charge. In Clause 18 we read:
"(a) on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding one hundred thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year or to both-

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
Under the old Petroleum Administration Act the maximum fine for a summary conviction was $200,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months. The prison term has been doubled. Similarly, for conviction on indictment under the old Petroleum Administration Act the maximum penalty was imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, whereas under Bill C-103 and the new energy administration act, the penalty prescribed is, as we read in Clause 18:
(b) on conviction on indictment, to a fine not exceeding one million dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years or to both."
I have registered my objection to these penalties before. It seems that if you are convicted for murder, rape or armed robbery you are likely to be back on the streets again in six months to a year, whereas if you refuse to pay your Petro-Canada tax you are fined $1 million and end up in jail for five years in the lowermost dungeon operated by those opposite.
When it comes to prescribing penalties under the law, it seems that those who would break the tax laws of this country are subject to much greater penalties than those who commit crimes against generally accepted moral standards of behaviour. I think that at some point in time we should take a look at the penalties prescribed under the Criminal Code for certain offences and then take another look at the penalties prescribed for breaking the tax laws of this country. In my opinion, the penalties for breaking tax laws are grossly out of proportion.
The second recommendation of the committee deals with a rather technical subject. It deals with overpayment in the EPF payments from the federal government to a province. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that we dealt not so long ago with this very subject when we were talking about writing off certain sums of money in cases of provinces having been found to have received too many EPF payments because their estimated population was below that subsequently established by the recent census. Provinces found themselves owing fair amounts of money to the federal government. In certain cases those amounts were written off. If an overpayment has been made under EPF, it can be counted as part of the refund on certain oil export charges which under the Energy Administration Act would be accruing to the particular province. It could deal with agency fees because I understand that the provinces, by reason of their collecting the oil export charge on behalf of the Government of Canada, are eligible for certain agency fees.
This is a technical change. It has certain advantages to it, despite the way in which I have explained it which was rather complex. It should simplify the bookkeeping somewhat and it should get around the problem which we very often have where the federal government gives a cheque to the province and three weeks later the province writes a cheque to the federal government. It should simplify some of that, at least in theory. It will avoid certain double payments.
For these reasons I support the change, but it is illustrative of the very technical nature of the legislation before us. It is extremely complex legislation. I imagine there are very few of us in the House-and even fewer in the general public-who could understand the bill clause by clause. It is technical,
administrative law designed for a very technocratic government.
Although I do not expect that it will be the case, I hope we can simplify some of the tax legislation. I am pleased to see the Minister of National Revenue sitting opposite. I am sure he would like to see that happen as well, but he probably suspects, even more than I, that it will not be the case. We find ourselves living with these very complex tax laws, rules and regulations which are very difficult to interpret. The more technical we get, the more likely it is that some technocratically-inclined lawyer will find loopholes in them.
I have another difficulty with Clause 10 of the bill which amends Section 17 of the act. It is difficult to read the new draft of Bill C-103 which was reprinted as amended and reported on June 1. Clause 10 amends Section 17.1 of the Energy Administration Act. Clause 10 becomes Clause 10(1) which deals with four subsections. If we go by the way the amendments have been printed, we come to the end of Clause 10 which deals with Section 17.1(4), and suddenly we are stuck with Clause 10(2). It is very difficult to find out to what that refers. The main difficulty is that subclause (2) is inserted, and it is the only one in the bill which does not amend a section of some other existing act of Parliament. Every clause in the bill, including the short title, amends the Petroleum Administration Act or some other act of Parliament but Clause 10(2) does not. It stands on its own, the way I read it.
If somebody wanted to make an update of all new legislation, he would take various acts of Parliament and all the clauses which amend different sections of different acts and apply them to the various acts. He would find that he had one subclause left over with no place for it to go. After all the other clauses were taken out and applied to the respective acts, we would have an act of Parliament comprised of one subclause. It is inconsistency in drafting, and it is very difficult to explain or to comprehend. Would it not be possible to rewrite or renumber Clause 10(2) so that it applies to the Petroleum Administration Act? It quite rightly belongs there. Then it would amend some section of that act and would not stand on its own in the middle of nowhere. This is a very technical matter which is best addressed by draftsmen in the Department of Justice. I hope someone in that department will read my remarks and take another look at it before third reading.
Now I should like to deal with what I perceive as the third major change recommended in the report on Bill C-103. It alters the wording in three clauses-Clause 11 which deals with the oil export charge, Clause 38 which deals with the petroleum compensation charge and Clause 44 which deals with petroleum compensation payments. Again this is a fairly technical matter, but previously compensation charges and payments were to be levied and made in respect of certain materials. Paragraph 65.19 of the old act gave the governor in council the power by regulation to designate certain products for payment or charges. Paragraph 65.19(a) allowed the governor in council by regulation to designate any hydrocarbon or mixture of hydrocarbon resulting from the processing
June 7, 1982

or refining of hydrocarbons described in paragraph (a) or (b) of the definition "petroleum" in Section 65.1(1) as a petroleum product. This did not include the possibility of a petroleum-like product such as synthetic crude oil produced from coal. In the first draft of Bill C-103 we see in a similar place in the legislation a redefinition which indicates that the governor in council may make regulations designating any product resulting from the processing or refining of hydrocarbons or coal as a petroleum product.
This so very often happens when we try to be more encompassing with our legislation; when we try to be more specific, we run into difficulties. There are certain difficulties with that definition. Thus, under the new proposal it was necessary to redefine what was really meant. The new definition has certain advantages. It indicates that the governor in council may "designate as a petroleum product any substance resulting from the processing or refining of hydrocarbons or coal if such substance is asphalt or a lubricant, or is a suitable source of energy by itself or when it is combined or used in association with something else." No doubt that is a better definition, but it still leaves us with certain difficulties.
In my opinion it would exclude certain things which should be excluded. Certain oil products should be excluded from the definition, such as aniline, benzene solvents, and various dye stuffs. Also it would exempt certain petroleum products such as solvents, plastics, and these types of things. This was good because we needed to encompass in our definition of these chargeable products certain coal products such as synthetic oil from coal to which I referred earlier. I understand that there is a certain amount of research being conducted by the Canmet division of Energy, Mines and Resources. I was pleased recently to visit that research establishment. I certainly hope, as do many other Canadians, that their research work proves successful.
It would also presumably include synthetic pipeline gas produced by hydrogenation processes, beginning with coal as a raw material. I do not know whether certain products will be included or excluded in this definition. In this respect we have run up against difficulties of clearly defining what is meant. First, coke produced from coal-where does that fit into it? Very little coke is used for heating purposes in Canada but there is metallurgical coke used. Where is the line drawn when metallurgical coke is put into the furnace, because part of it is used for the purpose of reduction and other parts of it are used at the same time as an energy source? Where would metallurgical coke fit into this definition? Where would water gas and producer gas fit into the definition? What about petroleum coke, which is produced in the process from which synthetic crude is derived from the tar sands in Fort McMurray, Alberta? I understand that there are large stockpiles of petroleum coke at the present time for which a market cannot be found. This is a good energy source which whould be used, but if it finds itself subject to taxes and charges which are proposed in this bill it would be very difficult to find a market for it. It is difficult enough now, and if it becomes taxable, as it might under this legislation, it will cause even more difficulties.
Petroleum Administration Act
The fourth matter arising from the committee report concerns the Canadian ownership account. It has somewhat broadened the scope of the minister to appropriate funds for public ownership. On this side we have a philosophical objection to the way in which the Liberal government has gone about nationalizing everything in sight and saying that it intends to follow on with that process. I will not get into an argument over that tonight but rather will just look at some of the details. Whereas the minister was formerly allowed to appropriate these funds for acquisition of certain investment instruments-debt instruments and equity instruments-he will now be able to use his powers of appropriation of public funds to engage in any form of appropriation. I do not know why the government has wanted to give those all-encompassing powers to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), but it has.
I am pleased to see that the drafting of Section 65.36(3) has been tidied up. We now have specific reference to an order which the governor in council must make when these powers of appropriation over the public purse are to be used. There are very complex rules and regulations which deal with a negative resolution on the part of Parliament when the minister desires to use these powers.
I must confess that I have read through about six times both drafts of the procedure to be adopted by the government and in Parliament when such an order is to be made. 1 find it very difficult to understand exactly how that process is to operate. If you read the proposals coming out of committee it seems that the proposed system has been watered down somewhat, that is if you go from the old draft of Bill C-103 to the new one.
As one illustration of that let me point out that the time period in which the government must table that order in Parliament has been extended from 15 days to 20 days. Originally, under the old draft, if such an order was contemplated and the government wanted to have the force of law behind it, that order had to be tabled in Parliament within 15 days of its issuance. That has now been extended to 20 days. We see a watering down of provisions there.
I Find it difficult to interpret this. One can contemplate many things that could possibly go wrong. Where does the House of Commons and the Senate fit into this legislation? What happens in the unlikely event that the House of Commons chooses to agree with the order and say that it is good for the country for the government to spend so many billions of dollars to take over the assets of certain companies to give to Petro-Canada, and the Senate says no? I have read through this on several occasions and I can envision serious constitutional difficulties which could arise if the Senate decides to take a different approach than the House of Commons on a particular order.
From a personal point of view, I would have preferred if the power of a negative resolution, which would have the objective of overthrowing an order proposed under Clause 65, had been

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
confined to one House of Parliament, which presumably would be the House of Commons since it generally deals with money items. Those items are not usually dealt with in the Senate. It is very unusual to give the Senate the power to address money items.
The last point that I can identify in the report which was handed down by the hon. member from York East deals again with a rather minor item. It deals with interest payments on petroleum compensation payments made in error. Under the first draft of Bill C-103, if the government paid a certain compensation payment to a particular refinery and subsequently discovered it had paid $100,000 too much, and that $100,000 remained in the hands of the refinery for a certain period, the refinery would be obliged to pay interest back to the government set at such a rate as the governor in council decided. I do not see anything particularly wrong with that unless the interest rate was set at a punitively high level. However, the recommendation of the committee in the new draft of Bill C-103 says that this interest will no longer be payable. If the government makes an error and pays the refinery or oil importing company too much money, it is the government's fault and it is out of luck. Of course it will get its original amount returned but it will not collect interest on that money. It seems rather unusual that the government itself has recommended in this particular case paying what is in effect a penalty since it will lose the interest that it might have received on that $100,000. It seems rather unusual for it to do that when one considers the UFFI situation where it has made a mistake but is not really willing to make any special form of compensation under those circumstances. In this case, if it makes a mistake it is in fact giving the oil importer or the refinery a bonus for its mistake. The company will be collecting interest on the moneys it has on deposit in the interim. I find it rather unusual that the government has proposed this. It is only a minor matter so I will not raise any great objection.
Now we come to the two motions which have been proposed by the official opposition. The first one deals with the petroleum compensation charge and the maximum amount of the charge which the governor in council will be permitted to make under this proposed legislation. We in the opposition have proposed that the maximum amount of the petroleum compensation charge be restricted to $28 per cubic metre. Believe it or not, it works out to 18 cents a gallon. I guess we must plead that we are somewhat guilty of nefarious objectives in proposing this figure of 18 cents a gallon. Your Honour will recall that some two and a half years ago, in the budget proposed by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cros-bie), the figure of 18 cents was the proposed increase to the excise tax on gasoline. Since that time, I believe taxes in excess of 90 cents have been imposed. The 18 cents we propose would be applied solely to the petroleum compensation charge, not to the myriad of other charges and taxes which have been levied by the government opposite.
When the vote on this motion takes place, I want to see how many hon. members opposite rise to vote in favour of a tax or petroleum compensation charge of $75 per cubic metre, some
54 cents a gallon. At the time of the last election they said that if the people of Canada voted Liberal, the taxes would never amount to 18 cents a gallon. I want to see which way hon. members on that side of the House vote on this very simple amendment we have proposed and put forward.
The second motion we have proposed is likewise very simple, but it addresses a serious problem. We propose that the amount of public revenue the government be allowed to collect by way of the petroleum compensation charge should not exceed petroleum compensation payments made to importers and refiners under this bill. We on this side of the House are scared because, as so often happens when the government first imposes its tax, it says that it will be applied for a certain reason, but after a while that reason disappears and the government still continues to collect the tax. In the case of gasoline, we can think of provincial road taxes which were first applied many years ago. The idea was to apply a tax on "motor spirits", as they were called in those days, in order to build roads, but after a while the connection between the two was forgotten and the taxes on gasoline were increased all the time. That money was not necessarily used to build roads. It just went into general revenue. This continued year after year ans taxes on gasoline are now a constant part of the Canadian provincial tax scene. They will never go away. If Your Honour will recall, the same thing happened at the federal level with income tax. It was first to be levied as a special charge to help fight the war, but then the war ended. Did the income tax go away? No, it did not go away. It has been with us ever since and it has increased and increased. We do not want this to happen with the petroleum compensation charge. I do not think there is the need, but if there were the necessity to have the charge and a compensation system where Canadian oil producers were taxed in order to bring imports for this country, we would live with it. However, when that need disappears, then that petroleum compensation charge should disappear. Our amendment is quite simple. It says that the two must remain in balance and that that particular tax should not exist any longer when the reason for it is gone, and should not be used as a mechanism to collect general revenue.
Those, then, are my observations with respect to Bill C-103. I hope that with regard to the two motions we have before the House, everyone will see fit to at least support Motion No. 5. It has been a pleasure for me to speak on such a technical subject.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Motion No. 6
That Bill C-103, an act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be amended in Clause 39 by striking out lines 14 to 17 at page 25 and substituting the following therefor:
"each subsequent month until such a time as the amount of revenue collected
under this section is equal to the sum of one billion four hundred and sixty

Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 6 deals with Part III.2 of the Petroleum Administration Act amendments, Bill C-103, which relates to the Canadian ownership special charge and taxation. During May of 1981, in violation of Liberal election promises, this sneaky little tax was brought in to finance Petro-Canada's purchase of Petrofina. In early 1981, at the urging of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), Petro-Canada made that outstandingly shrewd business decision to purchase Petrofina.
Mr. Speaker, as a player of the stockmarkets, you may recall that in the summer of 1980, before the National Energy Program, before the investment public came to know the true nature of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the ideologues who were advising him, the Canadian oils stockmarket was pretty buoyant. In fact, it was at a high, as some of us have learned rather sadly. At that time, Petrofina's stock was trading in the order of $50, roughly. Then some rumours started to spread. Apparently some believe it was more than just speculative rumours. The stock went from $50 to $80 or $85, even though the general stock market for gas and oil stock remained static and may in fact have gone down slightly.
About that time when Fina stock was going to about $80 or $85, the rest of the stock market in terms of oil was stagnant,
Petroleum Administration Act
perhaps slipping a little. Fina had not made any major discoveries. There is no other reason for the action of the Fina stock than that some people apparently knew something that others of us did not.
The government announced a takeover offer and then shrewdly engaged its agent, Mr. Maurice Strong, well known for his Liberal connections, to purchase Fina at the price of $120 a share. Those people who bought Fina stock at $50 in August were pretty happy. I do not know of anyone in this party who got wind of that information, but those who did came out rather well. The total price was $1,476 million. That was a very shrewd purchase for Canada. It did not create one new job for Canada, did not add one cubic foot of gas or one new service station or refinery. It did not add a thing to Canada unless, of course, the million dollar fee paid to Mr. Strong is considered an addition or the millions and millions earned by those who speculated fortuitously in the stock are counted.
That money had to come from somewhere. In order to pay off the owners of the stock, the money had to be borrowed. Borrowing costs at that time were in the vicinity of 18 per cent and 19 per cent. We had to borrow $1.5 billion at 18 per cent and 19 per cent to buy this company which had been paying dividends on its capital of about 2 per cent.
We did not gain any new jobs, an extra barrel of oil, an extra cubic foot of gas or anything else. For the same capital structure, we were paying 18 per cent and 19 per cent as opposed to 2 per cent. That was a really shrewd deal for Canada. For what cost us 2 per cent, we were now paying 18 per cent or 19 per cent.
Even though the assets of Petrofina were transferred to Petro-Canada, we could not burden that poor Crown corporation with the real costs of purchasing those assets, the 18 or 19 per cent. Heaven forbid! If they would have to bear the real cost, that would make their income statement and balance sheet look a little bit awkward. No, no, Petro-Canada could not be expected to pay the real cost. The consumers of Canada were going to bear the real cost.
Those little geniuses in Energy, Mines and Resources who invented the National Energy Program and the rest of this absurdity which has driven this country to its knees came up with the Canadian ownership charge. They said, "We are loading on all these taxes already, such as the petroleum compensation charge, the petroleum and gas revenue tax, the natural gas and gas liquids tax, the incremental oil revenue tax, the excise tax, the sales tax, the income tax. Who will notice the Canadian ownership charge-it is only four cents a gallon." It went on and nobody noticed. The Liberals broke every promise they had made during the election campaign. That was all right. A promise broken only hurts if somebody notices it. If nobody notices it, it is a great deal. That little four-cent a gallon tax went on. The little geniuses were delighted because it was politically successful. It was a great success. When Petro-Canada took over the Fina stations, they

June 7, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
rushed out and painted the dead maple leaf on it. The television cameras were there and the announcers were saying, "Holy smokes, we are Canadianizing."
The station was there before. The gas was exactly the same. You did not get any better gasoline or any more gasoline. No jobs were created. All that happened was that the consumer was paying four cents a gallon for the privilege of seeing that dead maple leaf on the new station. It was a real deal!
Those geniuses in Energy, Mines and Resources were so happy that they said they would allow the minister to raise that tax to 24 cents a gallon. Then they could buy four Petrofinas a year. We could then have these dead maple leaves painted on every service station in the country. They said that would make them so happy, it would generate jobs and make us self-sufficient. They said it would be marvellous, all the wonderful things that were going to happen.
With the passage of time we realized that the $1.5 billion we paid for Petrofina was at least a billion dollars too much. If Petrofina were still privately owned, the stock today, if it behaved the way the rest of the oil stocks are behaving, would be trading at $20 or maybe $30. We paid $120 a share for shares that today are worth $20 or $30.
It was a shrewd business deal. It really fills you full of confidence. You just wish from the bottom of your heart that the people who made that deal were in charge of the entire industry. If they ran all the oil companies in this country, wouldn't we be well off with those clever people? My goodness, we could have deals like that every day, paying $120 a share for stock that is worth $30 a share.
As things go it is not the habit of this government to admit mistakes or to apologize for blowing at least a billion dollars, and probably more, of public money. It is blowing it, just blowing it. It gathered it in taxes and sent it to Brussels.
If that money had gone to a Third World country in the form of aid, that would have made a little sense. Why, though, for goodness sakes, are we collecting taxes from the consumers of gasoline and heating oil in this country to send to Brussels? Why did we send a billion dollars of unearned income to Brussels? We did not gain a job out of that transaction, we did not gain a barrel of oil, we did not gain a cubic foot of gas, we got nothing. We just took $1 billion and sent it to Brussels. And, because we could not afford it, we have had to keep our interest rates high, to borrow back the equivalent of $ 1 billion from some place else around the world. So we have this shrewd little business deal worked out by the geniuses in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, it cost us $1 billion, it generated not one job and it contributed something to the higher interest rates that Canadians are suffering from. A few more business deals like that, Mr. Speaker, and we will not have one and a quarter million unemployed, we will have two million unemployed.
These central planners in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, who think they are so much smarter than everyone else in the country when it comes to energy matters, are no smarter than those central planners in Warsaw or in

People were paid $120 a share for shares running between $30 and $50. Now those Canadians sold the shares because they had no choice, but they were Canadian-owned shares and now they are Canadian government-owned shares. If there is anything which shows the difference between nationalization and privately owned, surely it is this. Of course these people received a pile of money through the sale because they owned shares, but now those shares are no longer owned by Canadians; they are owned by the Canadian government. That is the difference between Canadianization and nationalization.
I should like to review one or two of these other taxes. We have talked about so many of these taxes that people are beginning to wonder just how many taxes are involved in the National Energy Program. The NEP did not do anything to bring the oil industry into Canadian hands. As a matter of fact, it did the very opposite. Scores and scores of Canadians who owned small businesses lost them because of the National Energy Program. Is that Canadianization? That is what happened. The NEP was not very profitable to Canadians. It may have been profitable to the Government of Canada, but not to Canadians.
We can see the ill effects of the National Energy Program right across the land-loss of jobs, businesses going bankrupt and farmers going bankrupt. All these things have ramifications. The NEP must take responsibility for many of the bankruptcies and losses. It did not bring the industry more and more into Canadian hands; it took more and more of the industry out of Canadian hands, in fact some Canadian industries went out of the country entirely. I will refer to COC a little later if I have the time, but that is enough for now.
Let us look at the PGRT. On October 28, 1980, the budget of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) initiated the PGRT effective January 1, 1980, at the rate of 12 per cent of all oil and gas production. The federal-Alberta agreement of September, 1981, indicated that the rate of the PGRT would be raised to 16 per cent but that a resource allowance of 25 per cent of the price of oil would be deducted from the taxable revenue. This raised the effective rate to 12 per cent of the wellhead price of oil. This tax change was given effect in the 1981 budget as well. There we have 12 per cent of the wellhead price going to the Canadian government; it is just one tax.
Now I should like to deal with another tax which was initiated by the government, namely, IORT. In the federal-Alberta agreement the government settled on price increases significantly above those scheduled in the National Energy Program. The increment, that is the difference between the NEP and the agreement prices for 1981, was $2.50 per barrel, with a similar increment in 1982. For the years 1983 to 1986 the increment will be $3.75 per barrel. The IORT will tax back 50 per cent of this incremental revenue. While this revenue is not subject to corporate tax, it is subject to PGRT. In addition to the 12 per cent PGRT tax, we have up to 50 per cent of the incremental revenue coming back into the federal treasury.
Already we have a pretty good sum coming out of the industry, but then we have PCC which allows the government to levy a special charge on all oil consumed in Canada in order to pay for the equivalent in compensation which importers of world price syncrude oil would receive. The maximum levy was originally set at $1 per barrel, but in July, 1980, the government raised it to $1.75. In the 1980 budget the government rolled the syncrude levy into the petroleum compensation charge which was imposed on all oil in order to pay for the import compensation and oil sands production, including the special compensation charge used to pay for Alberta cutback oil. This charge is being levied as high as $8.15 per barrel. A scheduled increase for January, 1982, of $2.50 was cancelled. The current levy is $6.30.
Under Bill C-94, which would have been passed by the Liberal majority had we not started the bells ringing and kept them ringing until that bill was split into several bills, this charge could have gone as high as $20 per barrel. The maximum order of this levy imposed on oil has now gone down to $12 under Bill C-103. Let the people of Canada out there who thought that the bells were a game or something to amuse ourselves know that it saved them $8 per barrel on every barrel
June 7, 1982

of oil. This levy is imposed on oil as it enters the refineries, hence the oft-used reference to refinery taxes. That is the PCC. We have the PGRT, the lORT and the PCC.
There used to be a story in the old Alexander readers about the fellow who wanted to get all the golden eggs from the goose at one time. He killed the goose so that he could pick them out, but got nothing after all. This is what is happening now. The government is taking so much out of the industry that there will be no industry left. It is killing the goose that lays the golden egg. The government has already started to give some back. An hon. member of the New Democratic Party, its energy critic, said that he would like to know where the money came from. That $2 billion came from the oil industry, and the government is just giving some of it back. It should never have been taken in the first place. Killing the goose will not help the country.
Then we have the Canadian ownership charge, COC, which I have already discussed. Then there is the federal sales tax. The government originally imposed a 5-cent per gallon tax on gasoline and diesel fuel. The budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) sought to change the fixed rate to a 9 per cent ad valorem tax imposed on products as they leave refineries. Now we have a federal sales tax on the price of gasoline and diesel fuel. Finally we have another tax-perhaps I should not say "finally" because there may be some about which I do not even know-which is the excise tax on gasoline. This tax is a vicious tax indeed. The excise tax on gasoline was originally imposed in the June 23, 1975 Budget of John Turner at the rate of 10 cents per gallon. In November 1978, in an attempt to curry favour with voters in the pre-election period, the then minister of finance, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), reduced the tax to 7 cents in order to offset the impact of a crude oil price rise which was due to flow through to consumers. The budget of the hon. member for St. John's West on December 11, 1979, would have raised this tax to 25 cents per gallon. In the mini budget of the Minister of Finance in April 1980, the excise tax was imposed at the rate of 1.5 cents per litre, which is the current rate. This tax is refundable for those using gasoline for non-personal purposes.
That is a list of at least six taxes which are taking money out of the petroleum industry, yet some people wonder why the petroleum industry is dying and going bankrupt, why business after business are going bankrupt, and why some of them have even fled the country in an attempt to stay alive. It also tells some of the story that the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) told the other night about equipment costing tremendous sums of money being sold for a song because there was no use for it any more; it was being sold and taken out of the country, for the large part. This is supposed to be Canadiani-zation? What the government is doing is bankrupting the country.
Let us see what some of the people have had to say about this, people such as businessmen who have been successful through the years and had started from scratch. They started by using their backs and their arms, by thinking and by cooperating with other people so as to build up businesses. There is one chap, Ron Southern, who today is president and chief
Petroleum Administration Act
executive officer of Atco Limited in Alberta. This is a good company. I had business dealings with this company when I was involved with the highways department in Alberta. That company always gave dollar for dollar value and tried to be a good corporate citizen. This is what Mr. Southern said:
The Canadian government failed to recognize fundamental investment factors in creating the National Energy Program, and the result is a policy which carries the seeds of its own destruction, and will require substantial modification.
It will require this if it is going to survive. The absence of the oil industry itself at the planning table was very, very evident. In other words, the people who did not know the intricacies of the industry decided to tell the industry what was good for it and how it should operate. It is no wonder that there was an absolute and complete failure of the National Energy Program and, along with that failure, it has ruined many other parts of the country.
Mr. Southern went on to say:
The federal government tried to impose a program as though there were no other players in the game. It avoided debate by refusing to allow the oil industry itself a place at the table.
He went on:
One does not know for certain whether the federal government knowingly set up a possible situation that could eventually lead to a consolidation of the industry into a handful of huge petroleum companies, the majority of which are government-owned, or heavily influenced, or that the government genuinely did not understand that the elements of the NEP could produce such a result.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said this afternoon that he would give the government the benefit of the doubt. However, there are too many instances like this. We have seen where the National Energy Program has ruined one industry in this country. Now we have something similar happening through Bill C-85 which provides for the creation of Canagrex, a brand new corporation which is to have such control over the food and agricultural industry in Canada. It will even be able to tell the farmers what they can grow and what they can or cannot sell. What are we coming to? Is this government trying to get control of energy and then control of agriculture to make us subjects and slaves to it, subject to an all-powerful government? If it is not, then why is legislation like this being allowed by their own members who will suffer just as much as anyone once they are out of the House?
The people of Canada are angry and afraid of what they see happening. They are fearful when they hear about Canagrex. I received a letter of sadness from a lady who lives on a farm. She said, "It almost makes me feel as if I have to sell the farm and get out of the country." She said, "I am afraid, if our government is going to take this powerful control over the exporting and growing of food in Canada."
There is an attempt to do this in the oil industry and now the government is attempting to do this in the food industry. How much further will it go?
As Mr. Southern said, he does not know whether it was by design that the government consolidated the industry into a
June 7, 1982

Petroleum Administration Act
handful of huge petroleum companies, the majority of which are government owned or heavily influenced by the government, or whether it simply made a mistake. The government itself will have to answer that.
Mr. Southern went on to say:
NEP has done irreparable harm to the smaller Canadian-owned independent petroleum companies, the contract drilling and well service companies as well as Canadian manufacturing and supply companies. Ottawa will eventually be forced to modify its plans in order to restore lost confidence and revitalize the petroleum sector in particular and Canadian manufacturing and service industries in general.
The other night the government recognized that it had made some mistakes. It is giving $2 billion out of the $6 billion that it has taken from the industry back to it. That is not enough. It will start the industry rolling again to some degree but will do nothing for the consumer. It is not doing anything for the many consumers who cannot get jobs.
What are these taxes doing to our people? Let us examine the price of gasoline. Out of today's price per gallon of gasoline, 77 cents is federal government taxes. Out of heating oil, 40 cents out of every gallon is federal government taxes. I recently talked about the fact that people across Canada who are burning heating oil have had their bills go up, and 40 cents out of every gallon that they purchase goes into the coffers of the federal government. That is where the major charge comes from and that is what makes the big difference. The government calls that Canadian ownership. It is no wonder that the people of Canada are rising up in anger when they say, "You talk about Canadian ownership, but you are robbing me of my income so that I cannot even pay my taxes or my mortgage. I will lose my home and I will lose my business, and you call that Canadian ownership?" That is what these taxes are doing. The government has been entirely too hoggish. It is trying to get every possible cent it can from the industry, and it will not only ruin the petroleum industry, it will ruin the other industries as well.
This is true even in the farming industry. With respect to the excise tax, we urged the members of the House on the government side not to put an excise tax on farm products or food production, such as on fertilizer. Would they listen? No, they insisted on putting it on fertilizer and applying it to the price of food so that everyone who buys food will have to pay more. Home-owners, widows, old-age pensioners, the crippled and the retarded will all pay more because of that excise tax.
We even asked the government to wait a few extra days so that the co-operatives in Alberta would not have to go to the bank to borrow money, thereby increasing their charges and putting a heavier burden on the farmers. The government will not even give it an extra 30 days. It said that they can pay it. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs would not even recommend it. Those people in the coop came down here and gave sound arguments but could not get anywhere because the government would not listen. Nor would the Finance Committee listen.
Farmers right across Canada, from Ontario, Quebec, the prairies, the maritimes and Newfoundland, who use fertilizer are being penalized. That has been one of the factors which has caused the increased numbers of farm bankruptcies. All the government has to do is to look at its excise tax. Not only does it want to kill the goose that laid the golden egg, it is killing the entire country. It is time that it awakened to the fact that the people of Canada will only stand for so much. When Canadians get to that point, the government better beware. The people are getting sick and tired of this taxation, taxation, taxation.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-QUERY RESPECTING CONTACT BETWEEN ACTING PRIME MINISTER AND CANADIAN DELEGATION AT VERSAILLES. (B) PURSUIT OF CANADIANIZATION POLICY
THE ECONOMY-QUERY RESPECTING CONTACT BETWEEN ACTING PRIME MINISTER AND CANADIAN DELEGATION AT VERSAILLES. (B) PURSUIT OF CANADIANIZATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue the matter that I raised today with the Acting Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). It was obvious to those of us who were in the House today listening to the question period as you were, Mr. Speaker, that the Acting Prime Minister did not have the mandate or the benefit of the party line when he was speaking for his government this afternoon. As you may recall, I asked him what contact he actually had with Versailles. Did he have any knowledge or authority to answer for the government here in the House? Finally, I asked him how much longer it was going to take the government to come to the realization that it could not continue to use the national energy policy and the ill-conceived and capriciously administered foreign investment review legislation. The government could not continue to use these two devices to derive billions of dollars from this country while expecting the taxpayers to subsidize the falling Canadian dollar which was the result of these policies, with still more taxpayers' funds to keep it from falling to a level which the government deemed to be unacceptable. The Acting Prime Minister said: "I thought it would be normal for me not to get in touch with them"-"them" being his cabinet colleagues, I suppose, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan)-"not to take time away from discussions they were having with other people."
I think it is really a shocking situation and an insult to Parliament when the Acting Prime Minister in this administration will admit to the House of Commons that he has apparently had no meaningful contact with his colleagues who were participating in this supposedly high level economic
June 7, 1982

conference at Versailles, to which he has been referring for weeks in all economic questions as being the venue in which some results would be produced. I think that that is absolutely shocking.
The minister was then convicted by his own answer when he said, "1 thought that that was the right approach with regard to the causes of the present situation. I think it came out strongly, from everything in the press, that the crisis we are experiencing now is not only in Canada." If we are to take this literally, it means that the Acting Prime Minister, the spokesman for the government, only knows what he reads in the press, and he is here in Parliament not as an enlightened spokesman conveying to the people of Canada and to the members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition the latest developments from a highly touted economic conference; rather, all he is doing is stalling with old, stale press reports, until the Minister of Finance wends his weary way home again.
This whole business of the way in which the national energy policy is being administered, is very interesting. This debate directly follows from what has been said a few moments before and relates to the questions to which I tried to obtain some answers this afternoon. I do not wish to repeat what I said a few moments ago, but the paradoxes are certainly so striking that they must certainly be underlined again. This government is intellectually and, I suppose, practically bankrupt when it comes to advocating any new policies. It can only fall back on whining and complaining about what the President of the United States feels it is necessary to do to promote economic recovery in his own country, measures which appear to be having at least some success. I would like to say something further to what the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said some time ago, and it has been noted before in the House. There are areas in which hon. members in my party, and members in the New Democratic Party do not agree. We sometimes have a certain amount of agreement concerning civil rights and environmental matters. We usually take completely opposing stands on our approach to economic management in this country, but I think there is a measure of respect because of that. However, the government opposite stands for very little except expediency. It will embrace any half-baked policy as long as it can achieve a mandate during an election campaign. Then, when it must produce as it is now expected to produce, having convinced the people of Canada that our approach was wrong, it falls back and whines and complains and blames everything on President Reagan. It is really a very shocking situation.
In addition to the other paradoxes that we see implicit in this and in some of the other things which have already been said about the National Energy Program and the government's tug-of-war economic policies, I think the question bears repeating again in this context: just what is the national energy plan doing to its government's own policies? I come back again to what it is doing to the airline industry in this country. Again I repeat the submission which I have briefly summarized but which I believe to be accurate. It is the submission AT AC
Adjournment Debate
made to a committee of this House. I may not have put it on the record in its entirety a few moments ago, but I would like to refer to it again because it fits right in with the kind of information and approach many of us were trying to elicit from the government a few moments ago and this afternoon. This particular policy in the national energy plan has been characterized by ATAC as charges imposed on both foreign and domestic air carriers. As they point out, it was effective as of January 31, 1982, to be replaced by this new scheme that will be and has been explained in the House and in committee. They said this:
In our view, this governmental attitude is incongruous inasmuch as it seeks to legalize a charge which has already been judged by government to be in violation of Canada's bilateral treaty obligations and for which as stated above, government has already informed the foreign carriers that they would be refunded (to the exclusion of Canadian carriers).
How can any national energy policy be held to be rational when, on the one hand, it is driving billions of dollars of capital from our country and, on the other hand, it is discriminating against our own air industry, and when the Acting Prime Minister cannot answer for the government but only refers to press clippings and then begs us to wait until the Minister of Finance, who never had any answers before, returns from Versailles to enlighten us.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has given us the usual Tory Eaton's catalogue of haphazard complaints. His story tonight is that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has given him an inadequate answer, based on the fact that that minister has not incessantly telephoned the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in Versailles in anticipation of the hon. member's question.

subtopic: ASTRA TRUST-POSITION OF DEPOSITORS. (B) MINISTER'S STATEMENT
ASTRA TRUST-POSITION OF DEPOSITORS. (B) MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 26 last, investors in the Astra Trust Company were told by the

June 7, 1982
Adjournment Debate
Federal Court of Canada that even if they could prove negligence against the officials or the ministers with regard to supervision, licensing or inspecting of the Astra Trust Corporation, they would not be allowed compensation.
Since the Government of Canada managed to obtain compensation for itself, I took the liberty on April 26 to ask the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) what he was prepared to do for those individuals who had lost their life savings and hard-earned earnings in the collapse of Astra Trust. I argued then, as I still do, that this government has an obligation to those depositors because Astra Trust was incorporated by this government after it was refused incorporation by the province of Ontario.
It was through that incorporation that the subsidiary mortgage and investment corporations were established as wholly-owned subsidiary corporations of Astra Trust. Because it was incorporated as a trust company with whatever indications that trust really means, it invited the public to make deposits, and so they did. Unfortunately, it went through those subsidiary companies which did not have the protection of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
The minister replied that it was the fault of the province. It was the usual shifting of the buck which we on this side are used to. The minister's response was deceptive in that he led this House to believe that the federal government honoured its commitment to its depositors, that it was the Ontario government that left and continues to leave the suffering victims of the subsidiary companies without compensation.
That was the usual manly dodge on the part of the minister and his government as they peeled off the S29 million of the assets in the hands of the receiver and left a measly sum of less than $10 million for the benefit of the great number of individual depositors and claimants.
What this whole matter boils down to, Mr. Speaker, is the incorporation of Astra itself. We know of the heavy and constant pressure brought on the different officials of the federal government in the incorporation of Astra. We know also of the reluctance of those officials and ministers to appear before standing committees to respond to questions why it was incorporated and why it was so licensed to do business.
We know, too, that the people who were set up to do business by this government were one and the same group of individuals who carried on the business in those subsidiary corporations, and they carried it on fraudulently and dishonestly. Not only that, why should the government not bear some responsibility to those depositors? They set the rules. If you walk into a trust company, do you see a sign saying something like this-I do not see one when I walk into any such company-"Deposit more than $20,000 at your own risk?"
The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, a federal Crown corporation, one of many, reimbursed individual depositors up to a maximum of $20,000 each, for a total of $21 million. This was in addition to the repayment of $8,400,000
on a loan that they gave that same company to bail them out of financial difficulty-so that they knew they were in financial difficulties. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation then received 90 per cent repayment of those advances, which in turn took more than 90 per cent of the total of the assets in the hands of the receiver-adding insult to injury, Mr. Speaker. In fact, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, while others went broke, increased its deposit insurance fund by $33 million in the very same year it paid out the $21 million to the Astra depositors. In other words, the insurance fund would have in effect remained healthy, even if it had not received a penny or a single dollar in return from the Astra Trust when it collapsed.
In review then, Mr. Speaker, if this government has not a legal obligation to those victims, then surely it has a moral obligation to protect them in their life savings and hard earned moneys deposited with that company. First, there was the unusual and irregular incorporation which permitted-in fact, invited-the public deposits. Second, Astra Trust incorporated by this government did then incorporate subsidiary corporations, investment and mortgage corporations. Third, one of the reasons why the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was set up, was to guarantee the public and depositors against such an instance as this of collapsing or going bankrupt. No one could foresee then, and should not be able to foresee now or foretell, that there was the same deposit guaranteeing corporation on the ground, that would get its hand in there first, to the detriment of the depositors they were designed to protect.
The minister did not state his response in the House, but waited until he got outside of the House, to announce that there would be no return for those depositors. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there should still be hope for those depositors, there should still be a chance for them to receive some return; and the only person that they can turn to now is the minister in his capacity to ensure that the depositors in finance companies incorporated by this government are truly and properly protected.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for raising a very serious question that has considerable implications for ordinary people. I think that he has obviously thought out his concerns considerably in detail here. May I say that to the extent that the federal government had an obligation to Astra Trust depositors, such claims have been largely met.
