June 7, 1982

The hon. member has referred to an $8 million loan from CDIC to Astra Trust. This loan to Astra was made for liquidity purposes some time prior to the decision to wind up the company. CDIC obtained repayment of the loan by assuming ownership of the assets pledged to secure the loan. It is simply not true that the federal government received repayment of funds at the expense of the depositors. The federal government met its obligations to the depositors.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-PARLIAMENTARY REPORT ON BATTERED WIVES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
STATUS OF WOMEN-PARLIAMENTARY REPORT ON BATTERED WIVES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 12 I asked a question of the minister responsible for the status of women concerning battered wives. To the horror of Canadians, a number of male Members of Parliament responded with loud guffaws when I told the House that one in ten husbands beat their wives regularly. A protest from all parts of Canada has flooded in to all Members of Parliament. Articles and letters continue to express general outrage and demand redress on behalf of Canadian women. Unfortunately, since neither Hansard nor television cameras identified the offenders, all Members of Parliament have been shamed and must prove their innocence as a result.
Fortunately, this outrageous incident awakened a public and political awareness of the very serious and high incidence of problems of wife battering and the need for government action on recommendations which were made in the report on violence in the family tabled in the House by the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. The lip service we have had from ministers, and even from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), is not enough, however.
On May 12 1 asked the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), who had a secondary responsibility for the status of women, to initiate immediate federal action on this matter. Her reply was that she would consult with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to try to give some leadership to develop transition houses under the Canada Assistance Plan. This was quite unsatisfactory, since this would require provincial agreement, and the result would be inadequate funds. It seems the minister had not studied the report, which recommends that the federal government should take immediate federal action on its own to provide start-up funds and facilities for new transition houses. The federal government should also ensure adequate ongoing funding to maintain a core staff.
There are over 90 transition houses now in Canada, most of them inadequately funded and barely able to survive, and many more communities need similar and better services.
The minister responsible for the status of women also misled the House when she said she had discussed this matter of battered wives at her meeting with provincial ministers, when actually she merely announced at that meeting the report had been tabled.
I also asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) to take immediate action on recommendations concerning justice and
Adjournment Debate
law enforcement, and he bragged that he was training young RCMP cadets. The committee recommended, however, that there be retraining and sensitizing of all police officers to deal more effectively with wife assault, not just training of young cadets who have little serious interest or experience in domestic disputes. The Solicitor General also ignored recommendations for affirmative action in the RCMP, which is needed to provide male-female teams on the beat. He ignored the recommendation to have police lay charges against assailants, since this can rarely be done by battered wives who fear reprisals. A large increase in the number of federal judges was also recommended, to deal with exclusion orders and to protect spouses. The minister ignored all these recommendations. These are all matters of federal jurisdiction that can and must be dealt with immediately by the federal government to stop what is criminal assault.
CMHC is to be commended for providing low-interest mortgages and start-up funds to some new transition houses such as the one in Charlottetown. However, the report also recommends that CMHC initiate policy to encourage several units in every social housing development to be reserved as second stage housing for battered wives. These would pay normal rents, and as the minister need not provide further funding he must take action on this matter.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that last week I visited Anderson House in Charlottetown, a typical transition house which has had continually to scrounge temporary funds from the Department of Employment and Immigration, the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan), and receives inadequate per diem payments from the province. The staff has had to be cut by 50 per cent. This is a costly and inefficient way to provide inadequate funds which should be replaced by a federal advance of permanent core funding to maintain staffing and overhead costs of transition houses. The provinces could then contribute a per diem rate for each resident.
If we are serious about the problems of battered wives, the federal government must take these initiatives immediately. To do less is to continue to treat criminal assault as a chauvinistic joke.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-PARLIAMENTARY REPORT ON BATTERED WIVES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks by reminding everyone that when the subject was brought into Parliament by the hon. member opposite the question began as follows, "Madam Speaker, I have an upbeat question for the minister responsible for the Status of Women." I somehow think that might have been the subject of the laughter in the House at that time, rather than the content of the question.
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to respond to the question from the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) who has been a member of the committee studying the issue of wife battering.

June 7, 1982
Adjournment Debate
The commitment of this government on this issue is well known. In the Speech from the Throne the government stated that the serious problem of violence against women will also be addressed, along with other amendments to the Criminal Code, and efforts will be made in concert with the provincial and territorial governments to improve health and social services for women who are victims of violence.
The hon. member opposite may recall that both the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have stated that the RCMP now has, as part of their training program, sessions on family violence. This training is presently under review with a view to expansion.
Mr. Speaker, the problem of violence has been addressed by members of all parties of this House through the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs as a result of unanimous consent given to a motion by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). This motion empowered it to examine appropriate measures for the prevention, identification and treatment of abused persons involving intra-family violence and in particular to address the issue of battered wives and dependants.
The minister responsible for the Status of Women appeared before the standing committee early on in the proceedings and made a major, and widely reported presentation on this subject, and several of her recommendations made to the committee were very well reflected in the recommendations brought forward by the committee in its report.
The House may recall that a few weeks ago the first ever federal-provincial conference of Status of Women ministers was held and it was indicated there that this subject of wife battering is a concern of the provinces as well as of the federal government. The minister responsible for the Status of Women has assured us that the area will be examined more closely at the next federal-provincial meeting.
Also, the justice minister has promised that wife battering will be discussed at the next meeting of federal and provincial attorneys general.
In all the work that has been done on this subject, the great concern has been to bring this issue to the public attention. This report has certainly done that. The work of the members of that committee is greatly appreciated.
Mr. Speaker, I call on the hon. member opposite, and indeed, all our colleagues in this House to join together to help to protect Canadian women and, as Linda McLeod, in the report of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women termed it, put an end to the vicious circle.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-PARLIAMENTARY REPORT ON BATTERED WIVES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
